questions.text: What is the role of a Dockerfile?
options: Describing step by step how to build an image
questions.explanation: A Dockerfile is the recipe of instructions Docker follows to build an image: base image, files, dependencies and the start command.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a staging environment?
options: Testing a release in a production-like setting before it goes live
questions.explanation: Staging mirrors production closely so a release can be tested, including configuration and migrations, before real users see it.

questions.text: Where should secrets such as database passwords live?
options: In environment variables or a secrets manager, never in code
questions.explanation: Secrets belong in environment variables injected at runtime or in a secrets manager. In code, images or repositories they leak to anyone with access and live on in history.

questions.text: What does a lock file (e.g. requirements.lock) help with?
options: Reproducible builds with exact dependency versions
questions.explanation: A lock file pins the exact version of every dependency, so CI and production install the same packages and builds are reproducible.

questions.text: What is the main benefit of containerising an application with Docker?
options: It packages the app with its dependencies so it runs the same everywhere
It removes the need for tests
questions.explanation: A container image bundles the application with its runtime and libraries, so it behaves the same on a laptop, in CI and in production.

questions.text: What is continuous integration (CI)?
options: Automatically building and testing every change merged into the shared branch
questions.explanation: CI automatically builds and tests each change merged into the shared branch (and usually each pull request), catching integration problems early.

questions.text: What does a health check in a container orchestrator do?
options: Reports whether the service is working so it can be restarted or taken out of rotation
questions.explanation: Health checks let an orchestrator or load balancer detect an unhealthy instance and restart it or stop sending it traffic.

questions.text: What is a rollback?
options: Reverting to the previous working version after a bad release
questions.explanation: A rollback returns the system to the last known-good version after a bad release.

questions.text: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?
options: An image is a template; a container is a running instance of it
Containers are stored on Docker Hub
questions.explanation: An image is a read-only template made of layers; a container is a running (or stopped) instance created from it.

questions.text: What is a blue-green deployment?
options: Running two environments and switching traffic to the new one when it is ready
questions.explanation: Blue-green keeps two production-like environments. The new version is deployed and verified on the idle one, then traffic is switched over, which also makes rollback a quick switch back.

questions.text: What does horizontal scaling mean?
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling adds more instances behind a load balancer; vertical scaling makes one machine bigger.

questions.text: What does 'least privilege' mean?
options: Giving each user or service only the permissions it needs
questions.explanation: Least privilege gives each user, service or token only the permissions required for its task, limiting the damage of a mistake or compromise.

questions.text: Why run containers as a non-root user?
options: It limits the damage if the container is compromised
questions.explanation: If an attacker compromises a process running as root in a container, they hold far more power, and a container escape would yield root on the host. A non-root user limits that.

questions.text: What is a reverse proxy such as Nginx commonly used for?
options: Terminating TLS, routing and load-balancing requests to backends
questions.explanation: A reverse proxy sits in front of backend servers to terminate TLS, route by host or path, load-balance and add caching or rate limits.

questions.text: What is the purpose of log aggregation?
options: Collecting logs from many services in one place to search and alert
questions.explanation: Log aggregation ships logs from all instances to a central system so they can be searched, correlated and used for alerts.

questions.text: What is infrastructure as code?
options: Managing infrastructure through versioned configuration files
questions.explanation: Infrastructure as code describes servers, networks and services in versioned files, so environments are reviewed, repeatable and recreated automatically.

questions.text: Builds are slow: every small source change reinstalls all dependencies. What is the best fix for this Dockerfile?
questions.code_snippet:
FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
options: Copy package.json and the lock file and run npm ci before `COPY . .`
Move the CMD instruction above the COPY instruction
Change the base image tag to node:latest
questions.explanation: Docker caches each layer and invalidates it, and every layer after it, when its inputs change. With `COPY . .` first, any source edit busts the cache for npm ci. Copying only the dependency manifests first keeps the install layer cached until they change.

questions.text: Given this Dockerfile, which command does `docker run myimage --port 9000` execute inside the container?
questions.code_snippet:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
ENTRYPOINT ["python", "app.py"]
CMD ["--port", "8000"]
questions.explanation: ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable and CMD supplies default arguments. Arguments given after the image name replace CMD entirely but are appended to ENTRYPOINT, giving `python app.py --port 9000`.

questions.text: The image builds, but the container exits with `Error: Cannot find module 'express'`. What is the cause?
questions.code_snippet:
FROM node:20 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci && npm run build

FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
options: The node:20-slim image does not include the express package
The CMD instruction must use shell form for modules to load
Only /app/dist was copied from the build stage, so node_modules is not in the final image
The build stage must be the last stage for COPY --from to work
questions.explanation: Each stage starts from a fresh filesystem; only what is explicitly copied with COPY --from reaches the final image. node_modules stayed in the build stage. Install production dependencies in the final stage or copy node_modules across.

questions.text: A developer opens a pull request from a feature branch, but no CI run starts. What is the most likely reason?
questions.code_snippet:
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci && npm test
options: actions/checkout needs a personal access token
npm ci cannot run for pull requests
The workflow only triggers on pushes to main; it has no pull_request trigger
questions.explanation: A workflow runs only for the events listed under `on`. Here that is a push to main, so a feature-branch pull request triggers nothing. Add `pull_request:` (optionally restricted to main) to test changes before they merge.

questions.text: Why is it good practice to build the Docker image once in the pipeline and promote that same image from staging to production?
options: What was tested in staging is exactly the artifact that ships
Rebuilding for each environment is not allowed by Docker
Production images must be smaller than staging images
It removes the need for environment-specific configuration
questions.explanation: Rebuilding per environment can pick up different dependencies or base-image changes, so production could differ from what was tested. Promoting one immutable artifact keeps them identical; environment differences are injected through configuration.

questions.text: A pipeline step runs this shell script with `set -e`. What does it print?
questions.code_snippet:
set -e
false || true
echo "deploying"
options: Nothing, because false stops the script
questions.explanation: `false || true` is a list whose status is the status of `true`, so the command counts as handled and set -e does not exit. The script continues and prints deploying. This is why appending `|| true` to a test command hides failures in CI.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified with bash: prints deploying.

questions.text: A CI step runs the script below with plain bash (no pipefail option), where `false` stands for a failing build. What happens?
questions.code_snippet:
set -e
false | cat
echo "deploying"
options: It stops before printing, because set -e fails on any command in a pipeline
It prints deploying, because set -e only applies to the first line
It prints deploying, because a pipeline's status is that of its last command
It stops before printing, because cat fails on empty input
questions.explanation: Without `set -o pipefail`, a pipeline's exit status is that of its last command (cat, which succeeds), so set -e does not stop the script even though the first command failed. This is how a failing build piped into tee or cat is silently ignored.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified with plain bash. Caveat: in GitHub Actions an explicit `shell: bash` runs with -eo pipefail, which would make A true; consider saying 'plain bash without pipefail'.

questions.text: During a zero-downtime rolling deploy, a release adds a NOT NULL column without a default. Old instances, still serving traffic, start failing their inserts. Which approach avoids this?
options: Run the migration only after every instance runs the new code
Take the whole application offline during every migration
Stop running migrations in the deploy pipeline
Make migrations backward compatible: add the column as nullable, deploy code that writes it, backfill, then add the constraint later
questions.explanation: During a rolling deploy old and new code run against the same database, so each schema change must work for both versions. The expand-and-contract pattern splits the change into compatible steps. Offline migrations would cause downtime, and new code usually needs the new column.

questions.text: With this Compose file the api container sometimes crashes at startup with `connection refused` to the database. What is the cause and fix?
questions.code_snippet:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:16
options: depends_on only waits for the db container to start, not for PostgreSQL to accept connections; add a healthcheck and condition: service_healthy
depends_on must list the image name rather than the service name
The api service needs a ports mapping before it can reach db
Compose starts services in alphabetical order, so db starts after api
questions.explanation: By default depends_on only orders container start. The database process needs a few seconds to accept connections. Define a healthcheck on db (for example pg_isready) and use `condition: service_healthy`, or make the app retry its connection.

questions.text: Why do teams write application logs as structured JSON instead of free-form text?
options: JSON log lines are smaller than plain text
Each field can be searched, filtered and aggregated by log tools
Structured logs do not need timestamps
questions.explanation: Structured logs carry named fields such as level, request_id and duration_ms, so a log platform can filter and aggregate on them without fragile text parsing. They are not smaller, and neither encrypted nor timestamp-free.

questions.text: The on-call engineer receives about 200 alerts a night, most of them harmless, and has started ignoring them. What is the best fix?
options: Send every alert to more people on the team
Alert on every error line written to the log
Alert on user-facing symptoms such as error rate and latency, and remove or tune noisy alerts
Mute all alerts between midnight and 6 a.m.
questions.explanation: Alert fatigue makes real incidents get missed. Alerts should be actionable and tied to what users experience, with thresholds tuned so each one needs a human. Paging more people, alerting on every log line or muting nights do not improve signal quality.

questions.text: A request passes through five microservices and is slow. What lets you follow that single request across all of them?
options: Increasing the log level to DEBUG in each service
Comparing the average CPU use of each service
Restarting the services one at a time
A trace or correlation ID passed along in headers and included in every log line
questions.explanation: Distributed tracing assigns an ID to the incoming request and propagates it to downstream calls (for example the traceparent header), so logs and spans from every service can be joined. Log verbosity and CPU averages cannot tie events to one request.

questions.text: Dashboards show an average API latency of 120 ms, yet some customers report that the app often hangs for several seconds. Which metric should you look at?
questions.explanation: Averages hide the slow tail: a few very slow requests barely move the mean. High percentiles such as p95 or p99 show what the slowest requests experience, which is what these customers are seeing.

questions.text: A service exports the counter `http_requests_total`. Which PromQL expression gives the average requests per second over the last 5 minutes?
questions.explanation: A counter only ever increases (until a restart), so its raw value is a total since start. rate() computes the per-second increase over the window and handles counter resets. Dividing the raw total or taking max or avg does not give a rate.

questions.text: A team wants to release a risky change but limit the damage if it is faulty. They route 5% of live traffic to the new version first and watch the error rate. What is this strategy called?
options: A rolling restart of all instances
questions.explanation: A canary release exposes the new version to a small share of real traffic and compares its health with the old version before widening the rollout. Blue-green switches all traffic at once, and staging tests use no live traffic.

questions.text: What is TestClient (from fastapi.testclient) for?
options: Calling the app in tests without running a server
questions.explanation: TestClient runs the ASGI app in-process, so tests can call routes like a client with no server or network.

questions.text: What does `response_model` on a route do?
options: Validates and filters the response to the declared schema
questions.explanation: response_model validates the returned data against the declared Pydantic schema, drops fields not in it, and documents it in OpenAPI.

questions.text: How do you declare a path parameter?
questions.explanation: A path parameter is a {name} placeholder in the route path plus a function argument of the same name; FastAPI converts and validates it.

questions.text: What is a common use of FastAPI middleware?
options: Adding headers, timing or request ids to every request
questions.explanation: Middleware wraps every request and response, which makes it the place for cross-cutting work such as headers, timing and request ids.

questions.text: What does a dependency with `yield` let you do?
options: Run cleanup code after the response (e.g. close a DB session)
questions.explanation: A dependency that yields runs its code after the yield once the response is done, so it is the standard pattern to open and close a database session per request.

verification.reviewer_note: Exact timing of exit code relative to sending the response has changed across FastAPI versions (0.106 vs 0.118+); the cleanup idea is unambiguous, but 'after the response' is a version-dependent detail.

questions.text: Which is the right way to read an optional query parameter `q`?
questions.explanation: A parameter that is not in the path and has a default of None is an optional query parameter; str | None = None marks it optional.

questions.text: Where does FastAPI run a plain `def` (non-async) endpoint?
questions.explanation: A plain def endpoint is run in an external thread pool so blocking code does not stall the event loop; async def endpoints run on the loop itself.

questions.text: How do you raise a 404 from inside an endpoint?
questions.explanation: raise HTTPException(status_code=404) stops the endpoint and FastAPI turns it into a 404 response with a JSON detail.

questions.text: Why should passwords never be returned in a response model?
options: Response models define exactly what leaves the API; secrets must never be exposed
questions.explanation: A response model is the allow-list of what leaves the API; leaving password fields out of it prevents leaking secrets or hashes.

questions.text: Which ASGI server is commonly used to run FastAPI?
questions.explanation: FastAPI is an ASGI framework; Uvicorn is the ASGI server normally used to run it. Tomcat and mod_php are not ASGI servers.

questions.text: What does FastAPI use Pydantic models for?
options: Validating and serializing request and response data
questions.explanation: FastAPI uses Pydantic models to parse and validate request bodies and to serialise and document responses.

questions.text: What does `model_config = ConfigDict(extra='forbid')` do on a Pydantic v2 model?
options: Rejects input that contains fields not declared on the model
questions.explanation: extra='forbid' makes validation fail (422) when the input has fields that are not declared; the default is to ignore them.

questions.text: What status code does FastAPI return by default for a request body that fails validation?
questions.explanation: Request validation failures return 422 Unprocessable Content with a detail list describing each error.

questions.text: What is FastAPI's Depends() used for?
options: Declaring dependencies (e.g. DB sessions, auth) that are resolved per request
questions.explanation: Depends declares a dependency (a callable) that FastAPI calls for each request and injects the result, for example a DB session or the current user.

questions.text: How does FastAPI generate interactive API documentation?
options: From the OpenAPI schema it builds from routes and type hints
From a YAML file you write
questions.explanation: FastAPI builds an OpenAPI schema from routes, type hints and models and serves Swagger UI and ReDoc from it automatically.

questions.text: What is the effect of declaring a route with `async def`?
options: It runs on the event loop, so it should not call blocking code directly
It runs in a new process
questions.explanation: An async def route runs on the event loop; calling blocking code in it (sleep, requests, sync DB) stalls all other requests.

questions.text: Both routes are registered in the order shown. What does GET /users/me return?
questions.code_snippet:
1  @app.get("/users/{user_id}")
2  def get_user(user_id: str):
3      return {"route": "by-id"}
4
5  @app.get("/users/me")
6  def get_me():
7      return {"route": "current-user"}
questions.explanation: Starlette matches routes in registration order and the first match wins. /users/{user_id} also matches /users/me (user_id='me'), so get_me is never reached. Declare the fixed path /users/me before the parameterised one.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified: first-registered parameterised route wins.

questions.text: What does GET /items?tag=a&tag=b return?
questions.code_snippet:
1  @app.get("/items")
2  def list_items(tag: list[str] = Query(default=[])):
3      return tag
questions.explanation: A list[str] query parameter declared with Query() collects every repeated occurrence of the parameter, so both values arrive as a list. Without Query(), a list annotation would be treated as a request body.

questions.text: What does GET /files/docs/readme.txt return?
questions.explanation: A plain {name} path parameter matches one path segment only and never a slash, so /files/docs/readme.txt matches no route and gives 404. Declaring {name:path} would capture the rest of the path.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified 404 ({name} does not match '/').

questions.text: A client times out and automatically repeats the same request. Which HTTP method is not idempotent by definition, so a blind retry could create a duplicate record?
questions.explanation: GET, PUT and DELETE are defined as idempotent: repeating them leaves the server in the same state. POST (create, trigger an action) has no such guarantee, so retries need protection such as an idempotency key.

questions.text: A client calls GET /items (no trailing slash) and does not follow redirects. What does it receive?
questions.code_snippet:
1  router = APIRouter(prefix="/items")
2
3  @router.get("/")
4  def list_items():
5      return []
6
7  app.include_router(router)
questions.explanation: The router prefix plus path "/" makes the route /items/. With default settings Starlette's redirect_slashes answers a request for /items with a 307 redirect to /items/ rather than 404 or serving it directly.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified 307 with redirect_slashes default.

questions.text: Which request header supplies the value of x_token?
options: x_token, with the underscore kept exactly as written in the code
Authorization, as the default header for FastAPI parameters
None: Header() reads the value from the query string instead
X-Token, since underscores become hyphens and names are case-insensitive
questions.explanation: Header() converts underscores in the parameter name to hyphens (convert_underscores=True by default) and header names are case-insensitive, so X-Token is read. Sending x_token or Authorization leaves the parameter missing (422).

questions.text: What does GET /items/abc return?
questions.code_snippet:
1  @app.get("/items/{item_id}")
2  def by_id(item_id: int):
3      return "by-id"
4
5  @app.get("/items/{slug}")
6  def by_slug(slug: str):
7      return "by-slug"
questions.explanation: Routing matches only on the path pattern; both routes match /items/abc and the first, by_id, wins. Its int validation then fails with 422. FastAPI does not fall through to the next route when validation fails.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified 422: first matching route is chosen by path, then int validation fails; no fall-through.

questions.text: A mobile app may repeat POST /payments after a network timeout, and a customer must never be charged twice. Which server-side design best achieves this?
options: Switch the endpoint to GET so that repeated requests are always safe
Return 200 instead of 201 so that clients no longer retry the request
Require an Idempotency-Key header and replay the stored result for a repeated key
Raise the server timeout so that clients never time out and retry
questions.explanation: The server cannot tell a retry from a new payment unless the client labels it. Storing the result under an idempotency key makes a repeated request return the original outcome without charging again. Changing method, status or timeouts does not remove the duplicate risk.

questions.text: Which Pydantic v2 method builds a model instance directly from a JSON string?
questions.explanation: model_validate_json parses and validates a JSON string in one step (Pydantic v2). from_json, load_json and model_parse do not exist on BaseModel.

questions.text: What does this code print?
questions.code_snippet:
1  class Item(BaseModel):
2      name: str
3      price: float | None = None
4
5  print(Item(name="pen").price)
questions.explanation: price has a default of None, so omitting it is valid and the attribute is None. Nothing is coerced to 0 and no error is raised.

questions.text: With Pydantic v2 default settings, which call raises a ValidationError?
questions.code_snippet:
1  class M(BaseModel):
2      n: int
questions.explanation: Default (lax) mode converts the string "5", the whole float 5.0 and the bool True to int. A float with a fractional part such as 5.5 cannot be converted without losing data, so it is rejected.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified: '5', 5.0, True accepted in lax mode; 5.5 rejected.

questions.text: What JSON body does GET /item return?
questions.code_snippet:
1  class Item(BaseModel):
2      name: str
3      tag: str = "none"
4
5  @app.get("/item", response_model=Item, response_model_exclude_unset=True)
6  def get_item():
7      return Item(name="pen")
questions.explanation: response_model_exclude_unset=True leaves out fields that were never explicitly set on the returned model. tag only has its default value, so it is dropped and only name is sent.

questions.text: A client posts {"name": "pen"}. What happens?
questions.code_snippet:
1  class Item(BaseModel):
2      name: str
3      note: str | None
4
5  @app.post("/items")
6  def create(item: Item):
7      return item
questions.explanation: In Pydantic v2 a field annotated str | None without a default is required but nullable. Omitting note is a validation error (422). Write note: str | None = None to make it optional.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified 422: Optional without default is required in Pydantic v2.

questions.text: A client posts {"name": "pen", "price": 5, "discount": 50}. What does it receive?
questions.code_snippet:
1  class Item(BaseModel):
2      name: str
3      price: int
4
5  @app.post("/items")
6  def create(item: Item):
7      return item
questions.explanation: By default Pydantic ignores fields that are not declared, so the request succeeds and discount is dropped. Only extra='forbid' on the model would make it fail with 422.

questions.text: How should an API store users' passwords?
options: Encrypted with AES so they can be decrypted at login
As a SHA-256 hash without a salt
As a hash from a slow, salted algorithm such as Argon2 or bcrypt
questions.explanation: Passwords must be stored so that nobody, including the operator, can recover them: a slow salted password hash. Encryption is reversible, unsalted fast hashes fall to rainbow tables and GPUs, and Base64 is only an encoding.

questions.text: A logged-in user without the admin role calls an admin-only endpoint. Which status code fits best?
questions.explanation: The caller is authenticated but not permitted, which is 403. 401 means credentials are missing or invalid; 400 and 422 describe malformed input.

questions.text: What does the signature of a signed (not encrypted) JWT guarantee?
options: The payload is hidden from anyone who holds the token
The token stops working after the user logs out
The password supplied at login was correct
The token content was not altered since it was issued by the holder of the key
questions.explanation: A signature proves integrity and origin: any change to header or payload breaks it. A signed JWT is only Base64-encoded, so its payload is readable, and logout or password checks are separate mechanisms.

questions.text: Which registered JWT claim holds the time after which the token must be rejected?
questions.explanation: exp is the expiration time. iat is when the token was issued, nbf is the time before which it must not be accepted, and sub identifies the subject.

questions.text: A client calls GET /me without an Authorization header. What does it receive?
questions.code_snippet:
1  oauth2 = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="login")
2
3  @app.get("/me")
4  def me(token: str = Depends(oauth2)):
5      return {"token": token}
questions.explanation: OAuth2PasswordBearer raises 401 'Not authenticated' (with a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer header) when the header is missing, before the endpoint body runs.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified 401 (OAuth2PasswordBearer).

questions.text: The admin screen of a web app is hidden from normal users in the user interface. What else is needed to protect the admin API?
options: Nothing, because the route is not linked anywhere
A role check on every admin endpoint on the server
A longer, harder-to-guess URL for the admin route
A CORS rule that only allows the admin screen
questions.explanation: Anything done in the client can be bypassed: users can call the API directly. Authorization must be enforced server-side on each endpoint, for example with a dependency that checks the user's role. Hidden or obscure URLs and CORS do not stop direct requests.

questions.text: A user logs out, but their JWT access token (valid for 7 days) still works. Why?
options: The token is stateless and stays valid until it expires unless a revocation list exists
JWTs cannot be signed with a secret key, so logout cannot be enforced
The browser caches the token on the server side until the cache is flushed
FastAPI keeps every issued token in memory and forgets it only on restart
questions.explanation: A server that only verifies signature and exp has no record of issued tokens, so logging out on the client does not invalidate them. Use short lifetimes, refresh tokens, and a revocation or session check when immediate invalidation is needed.

questions.text: GET /orders/{order_id} needs a valid login and returns the order. User B can read user A's order by using its id. Which control is missing?
options: A check that the order belongs to the current user or that the user may see it
Hashing the order id inside the URL so that it looks less guessable
Requiring HTTPS for every request to this endpoint
Rate limiting the endpoint to a few requests per minute
questions.explanation: This is broken object-level authorization: being logged in is not enough, the code must verify access to the specific object. The other controls do not decide who may read which order.

questions.text: An anonymous client sends GET /admin?role=x with no token. What does it receive?
questions.code_snippet:
1   def current_user():
2       raise HTTPException(status_code=401)
3 
4   def require_role(role: str):
5       def checker(user=Depends(current_user)):
6           if user.role != role:
7               raise HTTPException(status_code=403)
8           return user
9       return checker
10
11  @app.get("/admin")
12  def admin_panel(user=Depends(require_role)):
13      return {"ok": True}
questions.explanation: Depends(require_role) forgets the call parentheses, so FastAPI treats require_role itself as the dependency: role becomes a query parameter and the returned checker function is injected as user. The checker and current_user never run, so the admin route is open.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified 200 {ok:true}: Depends(require_role) treats role as a query param and returns the checker function itself; current_user never runs. Subtle but fair.

questions.text: A server decodes incoming JWTs using the algorithm named in each token's own header. What does this allow?
options: Expired tokens to be replayed by exploiting small differences in clock skew
Cross-site request forgery through cookies sent automatically by the browser
An attacker can pick the algorithm none and forge a token that the server accepts
SQL injection through the sub claim when the user is looked up
questions.explanation: The token is attacker-controlled, so its header must not decide how it is verified. Servers should pin an allow-list of algorithms (and key types). This is the classic alg=none / algorithm-confusion forgery.

questions.text: A client with no Authorization header posts {"qty": "many"}. What status does it get?
questions.code_snippet:
1  oauth2 = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="login")
2
3  class Order(BaseModel):
4      qty: int
5
6  @app.post("/orders")
7  def create(order: Order, token: str = Depends(oauth2)):
8      return {"qty": order.qty}
questions.explanation: FastAPI resolves dependencies before it validates body parameters, and the security dependency raises HTTPException 401 immediately. The body error is never reported, which is also what you want: do not tell anonymous callers about your schema.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified 401 on FastAPI 0.142: dependency error raised before body validation errors are reported. Relies on internal ordering, but behaviour has been stable.

questions.text: Which design is safest for a password-reset link?
options: A random single-use token stored hashed that expires within minutes
The Base64 of the user id plus the time of the reset request
An MD5 hash of the email address of the account being reset
A 4-digit code that stays valid for 24 hours after it is sent
questions.explanation: Reset tokens must be unguessable, single-use and short-lived, and stored hashed so a database leak does not leak working links. Values derived from known data or short numeric codes can be guessed.

questions.text: In SQLAlchemy, which call makes the changes of the current transaction permanent?
questions.explanation: commit() ends the transaction and persists its changes. flush() only sends pending SQL inside the still-open transaction, refresh() reloads an object, expunge_all() detaches objects.

questions.text: Which SQLAlchemy 2.0 call loads a User by its primary key?
questions.explanation: Session.get(Entity, pk) is the primary-key lookup in 2.0. find and fetch_one do not exist, and Model.objects.get is the Django ORM.

questions.text: POST /items?name=pen returns 200. What does a later GET /items return?
questions.code_snippet:
1   def get_db():
2       db = SessionLocal()
3       try:
4           yield db
5       finally:
6           db.close()
7 
8   @app.post("/items")
9   def create_item(name: str, db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
10      db.add(Item(name=name))
11      return {"ok": True}
12
13  @app.get("/items")
14  def list_items(db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
15      return [i.name for i in db.scalars(select(Item))]
questions.explanation: Nothing calls commit(). The session only holds the new Item in a transaction; db.close() in the dependency rolls it back, so the row is never stored and the list stays empty. Add db.commit() after db.add().

verification.reviewer_note: Assumes default SessionLocal (no autocommit); close() without commit rolls back.

questions.text: The author table has 3 rows and Author.books is a relationship() with default settings. How many SELECT statements does this code send?
questions.code_snippet:
1  authors = db.scalars(select(Author)).all()
2  titles = []
3  for author in authors:
4      titles += [b.title for b in author.books]
questions.explanation: Lazy loading is the default: one SELECT loads the authors, then each author.books access triggers its own SELECT, 1 + 3 = 4 (the N+1 problem). selectinload(Author.books) would reduce this to 2.

questions.text: An async endpoint using AsyncSession reads order.items (a relationship) after the query and fails with MissingGreenlet. What is the right fix?
options: Close the session before the attribute is accessed in the endpoint
Call session.expire_all() right before the attribute is accessed
Read the attribute inside loop.run_in_executor on a worker thread
Load it in the query, for example with selectinload(Order.items)
questions.explanation: With asyncio, a lazy load would need implicit blocking I/O, which is not allowed. Eager-load what you need in the query (selectinload or joinedload), or await it explicitly. Closing or expiring the session makes it worse, and threads do not help.

questions.text: A module-level db = SessionLocal() is shared by all requests. What is the main risk?
options: The database refuses to open a second connection for the same process
Concurrent requests share one transaction, so they can roll back each other's changes
Every query runs about twice as slowly because the session is global
Pydantic validation silently stops working for the shared session
questions.explanation: A Session is not safe to share between concurrent requests: they would use the same transaction, identity map and failure state. Create one session per request, typically in a yield dependency.

questions.text: Which FastAPI feature runs a small function after the response has been sent, such as a confirmation email?
questions.explanation: A BackgroundTasks parameter lets the endpoint schedule functions that run after the response is sent, so the client does not wait for them.

questions.text: Two clients call GET /slow at the same moment on a single worker. Roughly how long until both have their response?
questions.code_snippet:
1  @app.get("/slow")
2  async def slow():
3      time.sleep(1)
4      return {"ok": True}
questions.explanation: time.sleep blocks the event loop inside an async def, so the second request cannot start until the first finishes: about 2 s. With await asyncio.sleep(1) both would finish in about 1 s.

questions.text: A nightly report takes 20 minutes and must not be lost if the API process restarts midway. Where should it run?
options: In FastAPI BackgroundTasks, because they run after the response
In a separate worker fed by a durable task queue such as Celery or ARQ
In an async def endpoint that awaits it before responding
In a thread started from inside the endpoint
questions.explanation: BackgroundTasks run inside the API process, so they die with it and have no retries or visibility. Long or critical jobs belong in a task queue with its own workers and durable storage.

questions.text: An endpoint does CPU-heavy image processing in pure Python. Which change most directly adds true parallelism across requests?
options: Declare the endpoint as async def so it uses every core
Increase the size of the thread pool
Add await asyncio.sleep(0) inside the loop
Run several worker processes, for example uvicorn --workers or gunicorn
questions.explanation: Pure-Python CPU work is limited by the GIL: async def and threads do not run it in parallel. Separate processes can use several cores. (Offloading to a process pool or task queue also works.)

questions.text: Which feature registers one function that turns a custom exception into a JSON response for the whole app?
questions.explanation: exception_handler maps an exception class to a handler returning a Response, so routes can simply raise the exception. The others do not provide that mapping.

questions.text: What JSON body does the client receive?
questions.code_snippet:
1  @app.post("/users")
2  def create_user():
3      raise HTTPException(status_code=409, detail={"code": "duplicate"})
questions.explanation: HTTPException's detail can be any JSON-serialisable value; FastAPI wraps it under the key detail, so the dict is nested unchanged.

questions.text: A production endpoint crashes with an unexpected exception. Which handling is best?
options: Return the traceback in the response body for easier reports
Log the traceback with a request id on the server and return a generic 500 message
Catch it and return 200 with an empty body so clients keep working
Catch it with except: pass so the logs stay clean
questions.explanation: Operators need the detail (logged server-side, correlated by request id); clients should get only a generic message, since tracebacks leak internals and masking errors as success hides failures.

questions.text: What status does GET /items/2 return?
questions.code_snippet:
1   DB = {1: "pen"}
2 
3   @app.get("/items/{item_id}")
4   def get_item(item_id: int):
5       try:
6           if item_id not in DB:
7               raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="missing")
8           return {"item": DB[item_id]}
9       except Exception:
10          raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="failed")
questions.explanation: HTTPException is a subclass of Exception, so the broad except Exception catches the 404 that was just raised and replaces it with a 500. Catch specific exceptions, or re-raise HTTPException.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified 500: the 404 HTTPException is caught by except Exception.

questions.text: A client calls GET /no-such-route, which no route matches. What JSON body does it get?
questions.code_snippet:
1  from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
2  from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
3
4  app = FastAPI()
5
6  @app.exception_handler(HTTPException)
7  async def custom(request, exc):
8      return JSONResponse({"custom": exc.detail}, status_code=exc.status_code)
questions.explanation: The 404 for an unknown route is raised by Starlette's own HTTPException, the parent class of FastAPI's. A handler registered for fastapi.HTTPException does not catch it, so the default body is used. Register the handler for starlette.exceptions.HTTPException to cover both.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified: handler for fastapi.HTTPException does not catch Starlette's routing 404.

questions.text: A client calls GET /search with no query string. What is the loc of the first item of the response's detail list?
questions.explanation: Validation errors report where the problem is: first the source (query, path, header, cookie or body), then the field name. A missing query parameter gives ["query", "q"].

questions.text: Where should a deployed API keep its JWT signing key and database password?
options: In environment variables or a secrets manager, never committed to git
In a .env file committed to the repository for convenience
Hard-coded in settings.py with a note to rotate it later
In the frontend bundle so the browser can sign tokens
questions.explanation: Secrets must stay out of source control and client code: inject them at deploy time from the environment or a secrets manager so they can be rotated and access-controlled.

questions.text: Which control most directly limits password guessing against POST /login?
options: Serving the whole API over HTTPS only, with HSTS enabled
Rate limiting by account and IP address, with backoff or lockout
A strict CORS allow-list that names only the official frontend
Hiding the login route from the generated OpenAPI documentation
questions.explanation: Brute force is about the number of attempts, so attempts must be throttled. HTTPS protects traffic in transit, CORS only affects browsers, and an undocumented route is still reachable.

questions.text: The users table holds ann and bob. What does GET /users with the query parameter name set to x' OR '1'='1 return?
questions.code_snippet:
1  @app.get("/users")
2  def find_user(name: str, db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
3      query = text(f"SELECT name FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'")
4      return [row[0] for row in db.execute(query)]
questions.explanation: The f-string pastes input into the SQL, which becomes WHERE name = 'x' OR '1'='1', true for every row: SQL injection. Use bound parameters, text("... WHERE name = :name") with params, or the ORM expression language.

questions.text: An API allows only https://app.example.com in its CORS settings. Which statement is true?
options: It is enforced by browsers, so a script on another server can still call the API
It authenticates callers, so other origins can never get data
It encrypts traffic between browser and API
The server rejects every request from other origins before routing
questions.explanation: CORS is a browser rule about which web origins may read responses. curl or another server is not bound by it, so it is no replacement for authentication and authorization.

questions.text: Any logged-in user can send {"name": "ann", "is_admin": true} to PATCH /me and become an admin. Which change fixes it?
questions.code_snippet:
1  class ProfileUpdate(BaseModel):
2      name: str
3      is_admin: bool = False
4
5  @app.patch("/me")
6  def update_me(body: ProfileUpdate):
7      user.update(body.model_dump())
8      return user
options: Remove is_admin from ProfileUpdate and change it only through admin-only code
questions.explanation: This is mass assignment: a client-writable schema contains a privileged field. The field must not be in the input model. extra='forbid' does nothing because is_admin is declared, response_model only filters output, and the HTTP method changes nothing.

questions.text: GET /preview?url=... fetches the given URL on the server and returns its text. Which risk is most serious?
options: SQL injection through the URL string
Any website being able to read the response because of CORS
Attackers can make the server request internal addresses such as cloud metadata (SSRF)
questions.explanation: A user-controlled URL fetched from inside your network is server-side request forgery: it can reach services and metadata endpoints that outsiders cannot. Mitigate with allow-lists, blocking private ranges and no redirects.

questions.text: A list endpoint accepts ?limit= with no upper bound. Which problem does this create and how do you fix it?
options: Callers can request huge pages and exhaust resources; cap it with Query(le=100)
Callers can inject SQL; escape the value by hand
Responses may be cached forever; add a Cache-Control header
Tokens may leak; rotate the signing key
questions.explanation: Unbounded page sizes allow unrestricted resource consumption, a classic API risk. Validate and cap pagination parameters, for example limit: int = Query(20, ge=1, le=100).

questions.text: What does this program print when it runs?
questions.code_snippet:
1  async def job(name, delay, fail=False):
2      await asyncio.sleep(delay)
3      if fail:
4          raise ValueError(name)
5      print(name, "done")
6
7  async def main():
8      try:
9          await asyncio.gather(job("a", 0.1, True), job("b", 0.3))
10     except ValueError as e:
11         print("caught", e)
12     await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
13
14 asyncio.run(main())
options: The ValueError escapes main() and the program crashes
questions.explanation: gather() re-raises the first exception immediately, but without return_exceptions it does not cancel the other awaitables. Job b keeps running and prints "b done" during the final sleep. Use a TaskGroup or cancel explicitly if siblings must stop.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified: gather propagates the first exception but does not cancel b; the sleep(0.5) lets b finish. Snippet omits 'import asyncio' (minor).

questions.text: One worker with default settings serves these routes. A load test fires 50 simultaneous requests at /a, and later 50 simultaneous requests at /b. About how long does each batch take?
questions.code_snippet:
1  @app.get("/a")
2  def a():
3      time.sleep(0.1)
4      return {"ok": True}
5
6  @app.get("/b")
7  async def b():
8      time.sleep(0.1)
9      return {"ok": True}
options: About 0.1 s for /a and about 0.1 s for /b
About 0.1 s for /a and about 5 s for /b
About 0.2 s for /a and about 5 s for /b
About 5 s for /a and about 5 s for /b
questions.explanation: Sync def routes run in the threadpool, whose default limit is 40 threads, so 50 requests need two waves (about 0.2 s). The async def route blocks the event loop itself, so its 50 sleeps run strictly one after another (about 5 s).

verification.reviewer_note: Verified: /a 0.23 s (AnyIO default 40 threads -> two waves), /b 5.09 s. Hinges on knowing the 40-token limit; option B is a tempting near-miss but wrong. Snippet omits imports.

questions.text: After every POST /export the client gets its response at once, but all other requests then hang for about 3 seconds. What is the cause?
questions.code_snippet:
1  async def build_report():
2      time.sleep(3)
3
4  @app.post("/export")
5  async def export(bg: BackgroundTasks):
6      bg.add_task(build_report)
7      return {"queued": True}
options: build_report is async def but blocks, so it runs on the event loop; a plain def task would run in the threadpool
BackgroundTasks run before the response is sent, so the worker is busy until they finish
Making export a plain def would move build_report to a worker thread and fix the stall
BackgroundTasks keep the request's resources locked until the task ends
questions.explanation: Starlette awaits async background tasks directly on the event loop, and runs plain def tasks in the threadpool. A blocking call inside an async def task therefore freezes the loop after the response. The route's own sync/async form does not change where the task runs.

questions.text: A single-page app on app.example.com authenticates with a session cookie. A page on evil.example sends a credentialed request with that cookie to this API. What happens?
questions.code_snippet:
1  app.add_middleware(
2      CORSMiddleware,
3      allow_origins=["*"],
4      allow_credentials=True,
5  )
options: Browsers reject the wildcard together with credentials, so the request is blocked
The API answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin "*", which browsers refuse for credentialed requests
Only app.example.com is allowed because credentials restrict a wildcard to the page's own site
The API echoes evil.example as the allowed origin with credentials, so that page can read the response
questions.explanation: When a cookie is sent, Starlette's CORSMiddleware does not answer with "*"; it reflects the caller's Origin and sets Allow-Credentials true. The wildcard plus credentials combination therefore lets any site read authenticated responses. List explicit origins instead.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified with Starlette: with a Cookie header and allow_all_origins+credentials, the response carries ACAO https://evil.example and ACAC true; preflight also echoes origin. Assumes the browser actually sends the cookie (SameSite), which the stem states.

questions.text: A user of organisation 1 requests /orgs/1/invoices/<id> with the id of an invoice that belongs to organisation 2, and gets it. Which change closes the hole?
questions.code_snippet:
1  @app.get("/orgs/{org_id}/invoices/{invoice_id}")
2  def get_invoice(org_id: int, invoice_id: str,
3                  user=Depends(current_user)):
4      if user.org_id != org_id:
5          raise HTTPException(403)
6      return INVOICES[invoice_id]
options: Make invoice ids random UUIDs, so they cannot be guessed
Look the invoice up by invoice_id and org_id together and return 404 when it is not found
Return 404 instead of 403 on line 5, so org existence is not revealed
Declare invoice_id with Path(min_length=8) so malformed ids are rejected
questions.explanation: The org check passes because the path org_id is the caller's own; the invoice id is never tied to it (an IDOR). Scope the lookup to the verified org. Random ids only hide the problem: a leaked or shared id still works. Status codes and format validation do not enforce ownership.

questions.text: This login-complete route tries to allow only same-site redirects. Which value of the next query parameter still sends the browser to another host?
questions.code_snippet:
1  @app.get("/login/done")
2  def done(next: str = "/"):
3      if not next.startswith("/"):
4          next = "/"
5      return RedirectResponse(next)
questions.explanation: A leading "//" is a protocol-relative URL: it starts with "/" so the check passes, and the browser treats evil.example as the host. Absolute URLs and javascript: values fail the check. Safer: parse the value and require an empty scheme and netloc, or map names to known paths.

verification.reviewer_note: Protocol-relative URL passes startswith('/'). A/B/D are rewritten to '/'.

competencies.description: Stateless and stateful widgets, the widget tree and layout widgets.

competencies.description: setState, InheritedWidget, Provider, Riverpod or Bloc.

questions.text: Which widget is best for a long, scrollable list built lazily?
questions.explanation: ListView.builder creates children lazily, only for items that scroll into view, so long lists stay fast and memory-efficient.

questions.text: What is a Stream in Dart?
questions.explanation: A Stream delivers a sequence of asynchronous events, such as websocket messages, whereas a Future delivers a single value.

questions.text: Which widget rebuilds when a Future completes?
questions.explanation: FutureBuilder rebuilds its subtree when its Future completes, giving the snapshot's data or error.

questions.text: What is BuildContext?
options: A handle to the widget's location in the tree
questions.explanation: BuildContext is a handle to the widget's position in the widget tree. It is used to look up ancestors such as Theme, MediaQuery or Navigator.

questions.text: How do you wait for a Future inside an async function?
questions.explanation: await suspends an async function until the Future completes and yields its value or throws its error.

questions.text: What does calling setState() do?
options: Marks the widget as dirty so it rebuilds with the new state
questions.explanation: setState tells the framework that the State has changed, which schedules a rebuild so the UI shows the new values.

questions.text: Which widget arranges children vertically?
questions.explanation: Column lays its children out along the vertical axis; Row lays them out horizontally.

questions.text: What is the difference between a StatelessWidget and a StatefulWidget?
options: A StatefulWidget has mutable state that can change over time
questions.explanation: A StatelessWidget is immutable and depends only on its configuration. A StatefulWidget has an associated State object that persists and can call setState to rebuild.

questions.text: What does `const` before a widget constructor help with?
options: Lets Flutter reuse the instance and skip unnecessary rebuilds
questions.explanation: A const widget is created once at compile time and can be reused, so Flutter can skip rebuilding that subtree when the parent rebuilds.

questions.text: What is a Future in Dart?
options: A value or error that will be available later
questions.explanation: A Future represents a computation whose result, a value or an error, will be available later.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a Key in Flutter?
options: Preserving widget identity and state when widgets move in the tree
questions.explanation: Keys let Flutter match widgets to State objects across rebuilds, so state follows an item when a list is reordered, inserted or removed.

questions.text: What does 'hot reload' do?
options: Injects updated code into the running app, keeping state where possible
questions.explanation: Hot reload injects changed source code into the running Dart VM and rebuilds the tree, usually preserving app state.

questions.text: Which widget lets children overlap one another?
questions.explanation: Stack paints its children on top of each other; Positioned places children inside it.

questions.text: What does the pubspec.yaml file declare?
questions.explanation: pubspec.yaml holds the package name and version, the dependencies and dev dependencies, and the assets and fonts bundled with the app.

questions.text: How do you navigate to a new screen with the basic Navigator?
questions.explanation: Navigator.push adds a new route on top of the navigator's stack, for example `Navigator.push(context, MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => Page()))`.

questions.text: Which language is used to write Flutter apps?
questions.explanation: Flutter apps are written in Dart.

questions.text: On a narrow phone this screen shows the error 'A RenderFlex overflowed by 84 pixels on the right'. Which change fixes it?
options: Wrap the Text in an Expanded widget
Add overflow: TextOverflow.ellipsis to the Text only
Wrap the Row in a Container
Put the Row inside a Column
questions.explanation: A Row gives its non-flex children unbounded width, so a long Text just keeps growing. Expanded (or Flexible) gives the Text the remaining width, which lets it wrap or ellipsize. The overflow property alone does not constrain the width, and Container or Column do not change the Row's behaviour.

questions.text: This screen throws 'Vertical viewport was given unbounded height'. What is the right fix?
options: Replace the Column with a Row
Set mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.max on the Column
Set scrollDirection: Axis.horizontal on the ListView
Wrap the ListView in an Expanded widget
questions.explanation: A Column passes unbounded height to its children, but a scrollable ListView needs a bounded height. Expanded gives it the remaining space. A horizontal list hits the same problem in the other axis, and mainAxisSize.max is already the default.

questions.text: The button is tapped many times, but the label always shows 0. Why?
options: The count variable must be declared final
A Text widget cannot display an int
The onPressed callback must be async
The change is not wrapped in setState, so Flutter is never told to rebuild
questions.explanation: The variable does change, but Flutter only rebuilds a StatefulWidget when setState is called. Writing `setState(() { count++; });` marks the widget dirty and shows the new value.

questions.text: A State object creates a TextEditingController in initState. Where should the controller be disposed?
options: At the end of the build() method
In a second call to initState
Nowhere; the garbage collector always handles it
questions.explanation: Controllers hold listeners and other resources, so the State that creates one must release it in dispose(), which runs once when the State is removed from the tree. Disposing in build would break the next rebuild.

questions.text: After `add()` runs, the ValueListenableBuilder listening to `items` does not rebuild. Why?
options: A ValueNotifier only notifies when a different value is assigned; mutating the same list does not
ValueNotifier supports only int and String values
add() must be called inside setState to notify listeners
ValueListenableBuilder needs a Key to rebuild
questions.explanation: ValueNotifier compares the new value with the old one in its value setter and notifies only if they differ. add() mutates the existing list object, so nothing is notified. Assign a new list, for example `items.value = [...items.value, 4];`.

questions.text: TodoTile is a StatefulWidget that keeps its own checkbox state. After the first todo is removed from the list, the checked state appears on the wrong rows. What is the fix?
options: Call setState when a todo is removed
Give each tile a stable key, such as key: ValueKey(t.id)
Declare the TodoTile constructor as const
Switch to ListView.builder without adding keys
questions.explanation: Without keys Flutter matches widgets to existing State objects by position, so after a removal the remaining tiles inherit the State of the tile that was in that position. A ValueKey based on the item's id ties each State to its own todo.

questions.text: Which call closes the current screen and returns to the previous one?
questions.explanation: Navigator.pop removes the top route from the stack. Navigator has no back, close or exit methods.

questions.text: A screen is opened with `Navigator.pushNamed(context, '/details', arguments: 42)`. How does the '/details' screen read the 42?
questions.explanation: The arguments are stored in the route's RouteSettings. The destination widget reads them with ModalRoute.of(context)!.settings.arguments (or via onGenerateRoute). The other expressions do not exist.

questions.text: After a successful login the app should show HomePage, and pressing Back on HomePage must not return to the login screen. Which call does this?
questions.explanation: pushReplacement swaps the current route for the new one, so the login screen leaves the stack. A plain push or pushNamed keeps the login screen underneath, and pop would just close the login screen.

questions.text: Why do many Flutter apps use a declarative router such as go_router instead of only calling Navigator.push?
options: Navigator.push is not available on Android
Routes map to URLs, so deep links and browser URLs work and navigation can follow app state
Declarative routers make screens load faster
Navigator.push cannot pass data to the next screen
questions.explanation: Declarative routers describe the navigation stack from route paths and state, giving deep linking, web URLs and redirects (for example to a login page). Navigator.push works on every platform and can pass data, so the other reasons are wrong.

questions.text: A user opens a picker screen and then presses the system Back button without choosing anything. What does this code print?
options: Nothing, because the await never completes
questions.explanation: The Future returned by push completes with the value passed to Navigator.pop(context, value). When a route is removed without a value, for example by the Back button, it completes with null, so the type is effectively String?.

questions.text: In current Flutter (3.7 or later), the analyzer warns about using the BuildContext after an await in this handler. What is the risk and the fix?
options: The await blocks the UI thread; remove it
pop cannot be called after an async call; use push instead
The context becomes null; assign it to a variable first
The widget may be unmounted during the await; check context.mounted before using the context
questions.explanation: While saveProfile runs the user may leave the screen, so the widget can be disposed and its context is no longer valid. After an await, check `if (!context.mounted) return;` (or State.mounted) before using the context.

verification.reviewer_note: context.mounted requires Flutter 3.7+; older code used `mounted` on State. Fine for current Flutter.

questions.text: `response.body` is the String '{"id": 1}' returned by an http call. Which code turns it into a Map?
questions.explanation: jsonDecode from dart:convert parses a JSON string into Dart objects (Map, List, num, String, bool, null). String has no toMap, Map.from needs a Map, and json.parse is JavaScript.

verification.reviewer_note: Assumes dart:convert is imported.

questions.text: This screen sends a new network request every time the widget rebuilds, for example on every keystroke elsewhere. What is the fix?
options: Create the Future once, such as in initState, and pass the stored Future to FutureBuilder
Add a Key to the FutureBuilder
Call fetchUsers() twice so the result is cached
questions.explanation: build can run many times, and each run calls fetchUsers() again, creating a new Future. Store the Future in a State field (initState or didUpdateWidget) and pass that same Future to FutureBuilder so the request happens once.

questions.text: The API omits `nickname` for some users. For those users, constructing the model fails at runtime. What is the cause and fix?
options: Map keys that are missing throw a KeyError; check containsKey in a try block
fromJson constructors must be async to read optional fields
json['nickname'] is null, which cannot be a non-nullable String; declare the field as String?
Dart converts missing values to an empty string automatically
questions.explanation: Reading a missing key from a Map returns null. Assigning that dynamic null to a non-nullable String throws a TypeError at runtime ('Null is not a subtype of String'). Declare the field nullable (String?) or supply a default such as `json['nickname'] as String? ?? ''`.

verification.reviewer_note: Strictly the failure is a TypeError from assigning null (dynamic) to String; C's fix is right.

questions.text: What does middleware mean in Express?
options: Functions that run in order on a request and can modify it or end the response
questions.explanation: Middleware functions sit between the request and the final handler. Each receives (req, res, next), may change req or res, and either ends the response or calls next().

questions.text: What is an unhandled promise rejection in recent Node versions by default?
questions.explanation: Since Node 15 the default for --unhandled-rejections is throw: an unhandled promise rejection is raised as an uncaught exception and terminates the process unless a handler is registered.

verification.reviewer_note: True since Node 15 (--unhandled-rejections=throw default); 'recent' is slightly vague but fine.

questions.text: Why use streams for large files?
options: They process data in chunks instead of loading it all into memory
questions.explanation: Streams process data in chunks, so memory use stays flat for large files and processing can start before the whole file is read. They do not compress or encrypt by themselves.

questions.text: What does `npm ci` do differently from `npm install`?
options: Installs exactly from the lock file and fails if it doesn't match package.json
questions.explanation: npm ci installs exactly what package-lock.json lists, deletes node_modules first and fails if the lock file and package.json disagree. This gives reproducible, tamper-evident installs, which matters for supply-chain safety.

questions.text: Which format do ES modules use for imports?
questions.explanation: ES modules use import/export; require() is the CommonJS system.

questions.text: Which runs first after the current operation completes?
questions.explanation: After the current operation finishes, the microtask queue (promise callbacks) is drained before the event loop moves to timers, I/O callbacks or setImmediate.

questions.text: Which module is built in for working with file paths in a cross-platform way?
questions.explanation: The path module builds and parses file paths using the correct separator for the operating system.

questions.text: What does `process.env` contain?
questions.explanation: process.env holds the process's environment variables, the usual place for configuration and secrets that must not be committed to the repository.

questions.text: What is the purpose of package-lock.json?
options: To record exact dependency versions so installs are reproducible
questions.explanation: package-lock.json records the exact resolved version (and integrity hash) of every dependency, so every install produces the same tree and unexpected upgrades are visible in review.

questions.text: What is the `worker_threads` module for?
options: Running CPU-heavy JavaScript in parallel threads
questions.explanation: worker_threads runs JavaScript in separate threads with their own event loop, which keeps CPU-heavy work off the main thread.

questions.text: What makes Node.js well suited to I/O-heavy servers?
options: It is multi-threaded for JavaScript code
questions.explanation: Node uses non-blocking, event-driven I/O, so one thread can serve many concurrent connections while operations wait. JavaScript code itself runs on a single thread.

questions.text: How should errors from an awaited promise be handled?
questions.explanation: await turns a rejected promise into a thrown exception, so try/catch around the await handles it.

questions.text: What does `await` do inside an async function?
options: Converts a callback to sync code
Pauses that function until the promise settles, without blocking the event loop
questions.explanation: await suspends only the async function, letting the event loop run other work, and resumes it when the promise settles.

questions.text: What happens if you run a long CPU-bound loop on Node's main thread?
options: Node moves it to a GPU
The event loop is blocked and other requests wait
Other requests keep being served normally
questions.explanation: JavaScript runs on one thread, so a long synchronous loop blocks the event loop and every other request waits until it finishes.

questions.text: Which is the safest way to build a SQL query with user input?
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries send the SQL text and the values separately, so input can never be interpreted as SQL. Manual escaping and concatenation are error-prone.

questions.text: What is the main risk of storing secrets directly in source code?
options: They leak to anyone who can read the repository or its history
questions.explanation: Secrets committed to source control are readable by everyone with repository access, remain in history after deletion, and spread to forks and CI logs.

questions.text: This script runs as a CommonJS file with `node app.js`. In what order does it print?
questions.explanation: Synchronous code runs first (A, E). Then the process.nextTick queue is drained, then promise microtasks (C), and only afterwards the timers phase runs the setTimeout callback (B). So the order is A, E, D, C, B.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified on Node 20.18: A E D C B.

questions.text: Inside the callback of an `fs.readFile` call, three things are scheduled as shown. In what order do they print?
questions.explanation: When the callback ends, the microtask queue is drained first (promise). The callback runs in the poll phase, so the check phase (setImmediate) comes next, and the timer only fires on the next loop iteration. Inside an I/O callback, immediate always precedes timeout.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified on Node 20.18 (5 runs): promise, immediate, timeout. Deterministic because scheduled from an I/O callback.

questions.text: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: forEach ignores the promises returned by its async callbacks, so main() does not wait for them. 'done' prints immediately, then the three timers fire in order. Use for...of with await, or Promise.all with map, to wait.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified: done, 1, 2, 3.

questions.text: Which Express call registers a handler that runs only for HTTP POST requests to /users?
questions.explanation: Express exposes one method per HTTP verb: app.get, app.post, app.put, app.delete. app.listen starts the server, and create and send are not routing methods.

questions.text: What does the built-in `express.json()` middleware do?
options: Parses JSON request bodies and puts the result on req.body
Sends every response as JSON automatically
Validates request bodies against a JSON schema
Converts the query string into a JSON object
questions.explanation: express.json() reads requests whose Content-Type is application/json and populates req.body. It does not validate the data or change responses; validation needs a separate library.

questions.text: Both routes are registered as shown. A request to GET /users/me gets the response 'by id'. Why?
questions.code_snippet:
app.get('/users/:id', (req, res) => res.send('by id'));
app.get('/users/me', (req, res) => res.send('profile'));
options: Express always prefers the route with the dynamic segment
The word 'me' is reserved and cannot be a literal path
Express runs routes in registration order and the first matching one responds
A path can only be handled by a single route per app
questions.explanation: Express tries routes and middleware in the order they were registered, and the first handler that sends a response ends the cycle. '/users/:id' matches 'me', so the more specific route must be registered first.

questions.text: Every request to this server hangs until the client times out. What is wrong?
options: app.use must be registered after the routes
console.log blocks the event loop until the request ends
The middleware neither calls next() nor sends a response
res.send needs a return statement in front of it
questions.explanation: A middleware must either end the response or call next() to pass control on. This one does neither, so the request never reaches the route and no response is sent.

questions.text: POST /orders with a JSON body fails with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'total')`. What is the cause?
options: The route should use app.put for bodies
req.body only exists on GET requests
express.json() must be called inside the handler
The body parser is registered after the route, so req.body is never populated
questions.explanation: Middleware only affects handlers registered after it. Because express.json() comes after the POST route, req.body is still undefined when the handler runs. Register body parsers before the routes.

questions.text: For an unknown id the client correctly receives the 404, but the server also logs `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`. What fixes this?
options: Return from the handler after sending the 404 response
Wrap the db.find call in a try/catch block
Call res.end() after the final res.json
Move the db.find call out of the handler
questions.explanation: Without a return, execution continues after the 404 and res.json tries to send a second response, which throws ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT. Writing `return res.status(404).json(...)` stops the handler.

questions.text: A router is mounted with `app.use('/api', router)` and contains `router.get('/users', ...)`. Inside that handler, what is `req.path` for GET /api/users?x=1?
questions.explanation: When a router is mounted at a prefix, Express strips the mount path from req.url before the router sees it, and req.path is the path part without the query string, so it is '/users'. req.originalUrl keeps the full '/api/users?x=1'.

questions.text: In Express, how does a route handler pass an error on to the error-handling middleware?
options: Return the error object from the handler
questions.explanation: Calling next with an argument tells Express to skip the remaining normal handlers and go straight to the error-handling middleware. Returning a value or inventing methods such as res.fail does nothing.

questions.text: What happens when this script runs?
options: It prints nothing and exits normally
The process crashes with an uncaught exception and 'caught' is never printed
questions.explanation: The callback runs later from the event loop, after the try block has already finished, so the catch clause is no longer on the stack. The error becomes an uncaught exception and terminates the process.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified on Node 20: crashes with uncaught 'boom', no 'caught'.

questions.text: What happens when this script runs on Node 20 with default settings?
options: The process crashes on an unhandled rejection and 'handled' is never printed
It prints nothing and exits normally
questions.explanation: load() is not awaited, so its rejected promise is not part of the try block and catch never sees it. Nobody handles the rejection, and since Node 15 an unhandled rejection terminates the process. Writing `await load()` would be caught.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified on Node 20: crashes with unhandled rejection, 'handled' not printed.

questions.text: What does this code print?
questions.code_snippet:
Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => { throw new Error('one'); })
  .catch((e) => { console.log('caught', e.message); throw new Error('two'); })
  .then(() => console.log('then'))
  .catch((e) => console.log('final', e.message));
questions.explanation: The first catch logs 'caught one' and throws a new error, so the promise returned by catch rejects. The following then is skipped, and the last catch receives the new error and prints 'final two'.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified: caught one / final two.

questions.text: Express does not use this function as an error handler and returns its default error page instead. Why?
options: Error handlers must be registered before all routes
Error handlers can only call res.send, not res.json
Express recognises error handlers by their four parameters, and next is missing
The status code 500 is reserved for the default handler
questions.explanation: Express tells error-handling middleware apart by its arity: it must declare four parameters (err, req, res, next), even if next is unused. With three parameters it is treated as ordinary middleware. Error handlers belong after the routes.

questions.text: How should an API store user passwords?
options: Hash them once with SHA-256 without a salt
Encrypt them with AES using a key kept in an environment variable
Encode them with Base64 in the database
Hash them with a slow salted algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2
questions.explanation: Passwords need a deliberately slow, salted password-hashing function so stolen hashes are expensive to crack. A fast unsalted hash is easy to brute-force, and encrypted or encoded passwords can be recovered.

questions.text: A route serves uploaded files by name. Which change is the most robust protection against path traversal such as `../../etc/passwd`?
options: Resolve the full path and reject it unless it starts inside UPLOAD_DIR
Remove the first occurrence of '../' from the name
Reject names that contain the word 'etc'
Wrap the name in encodeURIComponent before joining
questions.explanation: path.join normalises the '..' segments, so the result can leave UPLOAD_DIR. Resolving to an absolute path and checking that it stays under the base directory is reliable. Stripping '../' once can be bypassed with input like '....//', and keyword blocklists miss other targets.

questions.text: A server merges parsed JSON from a request into an object using this function. After the attack payload below is processed, what does `console.log({}.admin)` print?
questions.explanation: JSON.parse creates an own property named __proto__. The recursive merge then reads target['__proto__'], which is Object.prototype, and writes admin onto it. Every object now inherits admin: true. This is prototype pollution; block __proto__, constructor and prototype keys.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified on Node 20: prints true (prototype pollution via for-in over own __proto__ key from JSON.parse).
