questions.text: Which isolation level is PostgreSQL's default?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL's default isolation level is READ COMMITTED: each statement sees the data committed before that statement started. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE must be requested explicitly, and READ UNCOMMITTED is accepted but behaves like READ COMMITTED.

questions.text: What is VACUUM used for?
options: Reclaiming space from dead row versions and updating visibility information
questions.explanation: UPDATE and DELETE leave dead row versions behind (MVCC). VACUUM makes that space reusable and updates the visibility map and statistics; autovacuum normally runs it. It does not create indexes, back up data or drop tables.

questions.text: What does row-level security (RLS) do?
options: Restricts which rows a role can see or change using policies
questions.explanation: With row-level security enabled, policies decide which rows a role may see (USING) or write (WITH CHECK). It restricts access; it does not encrypt, compress or log anything.

questions.text: What kind of index is the default in PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: CREATE INDEX without USING builds a B-tree, which suits equality and range lookups and ordering. Hash, GIN and BRIN are chosen explicitly for special cases.

questions.text: What does EXPLAIN ANALYZE show?
options: The executed query plan with actual timings and row counts
questions.explanation: EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the statement and shows the chosen plan with real timings and row counts next to the estimates. Plain EXPLAIN shows only the plan and estimates.

questions.text: What does a transaction's ROLLBACK do?
options: Undoes all changes made in the transaction
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK ends the transaction and discards every change it made; COMMIT is the opposite. It does not restart the server or vacuum anything.

questions.text: What does `timestamptz` store?
options: A timestamp with an absolute point in time (converted to UTC internally)
questions.explanation: timestamptz stores an absolute instant (internally UTC) and converts to and from the session time zone on input and output. It does not store the zone itself. timestamp (without zone) stores a wall-clock value.

questions.text: What is a CTE (WITH query)?
options: A temporary named result set used within a single query
questions.explanation: A common table expression (WITH name AS (...)) defines a named result set that exists only for the one statement it belongs to, which makes complex queries easier to read and allows recursion.

questions.text: What does a PRIMARY KEY guarantee?
options: Values are unique and not null
The column is indexed for full-text search
questions.explanation: A PRIMARY KEY is UNIQUE plus NOT NULL, and PostgreSQL builds a unique B-tree index to enforce it. It does not sort the table, encrypt values or create a full-text index.

questions.text: What does SELECT … FOR UPDATE do?
options: Locks the selected rows until the transaction ends
questions.explanation: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes row-level locks on the returned rows until the transaction ends, so other writers (or other FOR UPDATE readers) wait. It does not modify rows itself.

questions.text: What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
options: LEFT JOIN keeps rows from the left table even without a match
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN returns only rows with a match on both sides; LEFT JOIN also returns every left-table row, with NULLs for the right-hand columns when nothing matches. Neither is always faster and neither removes duplicates.

verification.reviewer_note: Option C 'None' is a throwaway distractor; question is fine but very easy.

questions.text: Which type should store money exactly in PostgreSQL?
options: numeric or integer minor units (e.g. paisa)
questions.explanation: Money must be exact. numeric(p,s) or integer minor units (paisa) are exact; real and double precision are binary floating point and give rounding errors; text cannot be summed safely.

questions.text: What does a CHECK constraint do?
options: Validates that column values satisfy a condition
questions.explanation: A CHECK constraint rejects any row whose values make the condition false (NULL results pass). It is not an index, encryption or a foreign key.

questions.text: What is the safest way to pass user input into a query?
questions.explanation: Bound (parameterised) queries send the SQL text and the values separately, so input can never change the statement's structure. String formatting and hand escaping are error-prone and the classic cause of SQL injection.

questions.text: Which index type is typically used for full-text search vectors (tsvector)?
questions.explanation: GIN (an inverted index) is the usual choice for tsvector columns because it maps each lexeme to the rows containing it. B-tree and hash indexes cannot answer full-text match queries; GiST is a less common alternative.

verification.reviewer_note: GiST also indexes tsvector, but it is not an option; GIN is the typical choice.

questions.text: What does a FOREIGN KEY constraint enforce?
options: That a value exists in the referenced table
questions.explanation: A FOREIGN KEY requires each value in the referencing column to exist in the referenced table's key (or be NULL). It does not make values unique, set a default or speed up queries.

questions.text: In an online shop every order has many line items, and each line item belongs to exactly one order. How is this one-to-many relationship modelled in PostgreSQL?
options: Give orders an item_id column that references line_items(id)
Store the line item ids in a comma-separated text column on orders
Copy all the order columns into every line_items row
Give line_items an order_id column that references orders(id)
questions.explanation: The foreign key goes on the 'many' side: each line item row points at its one order. A key on orders would allow only one item per order; comma-separated lists and copied columns break integrity and normalisation.

questions.text: Students can enrol in many courses, and every course has many students. What is the standard way to model this many-to-many relationship?
options: A junction table with a foreign key to each of the two tables
A foreign key column on the students table only
An array of course names stored in a text column on students
Two tables that share the same primary key values
questions.explanation: A many-to-many relationship needs a third (junction) table with one row per pair, holding foreign keys to both sides, usually with a composite primary key. A single foreign key can express only one-to-many.

questions.text: A column is declared numeric(6,2) and the value 1234.567 is inserted. What does the SELECT on line 3 return?
questions.explanation: numeric(6,2) allows 6 digits in total with 2 after the point, so up to 9999.99. The input 1234.567 fits and is rounded (not truncated) to scale 2, giving 1234.57. An overflow error would need 5 digits before the point.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified on PG16: 1234.57.

questions.text: A shop prints invoices for orders placed months ago, and product prices change from time to time. Which design keeps old invoices correct?
options: Join order_items to products.price whenever an invoice is printed
Update every existing order_items row whenever products.price changes
Keep one price on products and add a printed_at column to invoices
Copy the unit price into each order_items row when the order is placed
questions.explanation: An order must record the price that was agreed at purchase time, so the price is copied (snapshotted) into the order row. Joining to the live price, or rewriting old rows, changes history; a printed_at timestamp does not preserve the price.

questions.text: A customers table has the columns customer_id (primary key), name, postal_code and delivery_zone. delivery_zone is always determined by postal_code, and many customers share a postal code. What is the problem and the usual fix?
options: It breaks third normal form; move delivery_zone into a table keyed by postal_code
It breaks first normal form; split name into first and last name
It breaks second normal form; give the table a composite primary key
There is no problem; every non-key column belongs to the customer row
questions.explanation: delivery_zone depends on postal_code, which is not the key: a transitive dependency, so third normal form is violated and the zone is repeated for every customer in a postal code. Second normal form concerns partial dependencies on composite keys.

verification.reviewer_note: Wording slightly imprecise: postal_code normally stays on customers as a FK to the new postal_codes table; only delivery_zone moves. Still clearly the best option.

questions.text: A tickets table uses a GENERATED ALWAYS identity column. What happens when line 5 runs?
options: It succeeds, ignores the 10 and stores id 1
It succeeds and the next generated id becomes 11
It fails because a non-DEFAULT value cannot be inserted into an identity column
questions.explanation: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY rejects explicit values unless OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE is given (error 428C9). Only GENERATED BY DEFAULT accepts an explicit id, and even then the sequence is not advanced by it.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified on PG16.

questions.text: After an insert that was skipped by ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, which id does the statement on line 4 return?
questions.explanation: The default nextval('tags_id_seq') is evaluated before the conflict check, so the ignored insert on line 3 still consumes id 2. Sequences are not gapless and are never rolled back, so 'db' gets 3.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified on PG16: returns 3 (the skipped insert consumed a sequence value).

questions.text: A catalogue has products with common columns (name, price), but each category has different optional attributes such as screen size or fabric. Which feature suits the varying attributes best, without changing the schema for each new attribute?
options: A text column holding a JSON string, searched with LIKE
A jsonb column, with a GIN index if you filter inside it
One extra nullable column for every attribute of every category
A new table per product whose columns are that product's attributes
questions.explanation: jsonb stores flexible, structured attributes next to the relational columns and can be indexed (GIN) and queried with operators. Extra columns or tables need a schema change per attribute, and LIKE over a text string cannot use an index well.

questions.text: A score column holds 10, NULL and 30. What does the SELECT on line 3 return?
questions.explanation: count(*) counts rows (3) while count(score) counts only non-NULL values (2), so the result is the single row 3, 2.

questions.text: You want only the departments that have more than five employees. Which clause filters on the result of count(*) after grouping?
questions.explanation: HAVING filters groups after aggregation. WHERE runs before grouping and cannot contain aggregates; ORDER BY only sorts; QUALIFY exists in some other databases but not in PostgreSQL.

questions.text: A LEFT JOIN is followed by a WHERE condition on a column of the right table. What does this query return?
questions.explanation: The LEFT JOIN yields (1,NULL), (2,2), (3,3), but the WHERE clause runs after the join: b.id > 2 is false or NULL for the first two rows, leaving only (3,3). Filtering the right table in WHERE turns the LEFT JOIN into an inner join.

questions.text: Which approach correctly lists the customers who have never placed an order?
options: INNER JOIN orders on customer_id, then keep rows WHERE orders.id IS NULL
LEFT JOIN orders on customer_id, then keep rows WHERE orders.id IS NULL
LEFT JOIN orders on customer_id, then keep rows WHERE orders.id = NULL
LEFT JOIN orders on customer_id, then GROUP BY customers.id HAVING count(*) = 0
questions.explanation: Unmatched customers get NULLs from the LEFT JOIN, and IS NULL finds them. An INNER JOIN drops them first, '= NULL' is never true, and count(*) counts the NULL-extended row as 1, so a group can never have 0.

questions.text: The subquery on line 5 yields a NULL among its values. What does the NOT IN query return?
questions.explanation: id NOT IN (2, NULL) is NULL for ids 1 and 3 (the comparison with NULL is unknown) and false for 2, so no row qualifies and the count is 0. NOT EXISTS or filtering NULLs out of the subquery avoids this trap.

questions.text: Two students tie for the highest score. In which sequence does the rank() query return the values of r?
questions.explanation: rank() gives tied rows the same rank and then skips: 90, 90, 80, 70 become 1, 1, 3, 4. row_number() would give 1, 2, 3, 4 and dense_rank() would give 1, 1, 2, 3.

questions.text: The table payments has no rows for user 999. What does SELECT sum(amount) FROM payments WHERE user_id = 999 return?
options: An error about an empty group
questions.explanation: An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns exactly one row. sum() over zero rows is NULL (only count() returns 0), so use COALESCE(sum(amount), 0) when a zero is wanted.

questions.text: Which rows does the DISTINCT ON query return as (customer_id, total)?
questions.explanation: DISTINCT ON (customer_id) keeps the first row of each customer in the ORDER BY order, here the newest created_on: (1, 20) from 2024-01-03 and (2, 5) from 2024-01-02. It does not pick the largest total.

questions.text: A UNIQUE column receives two NULL values on line 2. What is the outcome of the three statements?
options: Line 2 fails with a unique violation because of the two NULLs
Line 2 succeeds and the SELECT returns 2, because duplicate NULLs are merged
Line 2 succeeds and the SELECT returns 1, because only non-NULL values are stored
Line 2 succeeds and the SELECT returns 3
questions.explanation: NULL is never equal to NULL, so a UNIQUE constraint allows any number of NULLs (unless NULLS NOT DISTINCT is specified, PostgreSQL 15+). All three rows are stored.

verification.reviewer_note: Correct for PG16 default (NULLS DISTINCT); would differ only with NULLS NOT DISTINCT (PG15+), which is not used here.

questions.text: After the DELETE on line 8 removes a parent that has two child rows, what does the SELECT on line 9 return?
questions.explanation: ON DELETE CASCADE deletes the child rows that reference the deleted parent: rows 10 and 11 go with parent 1, leaving only row 12.

questions.text: A CHECK (price > 0) column receives NULL. What happens when line 2 runs?
questions.code_snippet:
1  CREATE TABLE items (price int CHECK (price > 0));
2  INSERT INTO items VALUES (NULL);
options: It fails with a check constraint violation
It succeeds and stores a NULL price
It fails with a not-null violation
questions.explanation: A CHECK constraint rejects a row only when the condition is false. NULL > 0 evaluates to NULL (unknown), which passes. Add NOT NULL as well if a price must always be present.

questions.text: A foreign key is DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED and the child row is inserted before its parent. Which statement fails, if any?
options: Line 7, because parent 5 does not exist yet
Line 8, because the child row already exists
Line 9, because the commit is rejected
None; the foreign key is checked at COMMIT and then passes
questions.explanation: A DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED constraint is checked at COMMIT, not per statement. By then parent 5 exists, so every statement succeeds. Without DEFERRABLE, line 7 would fail immediately.

questions.text: Each user may have at most one subscription with status 'active', but any number of 'cancelled' or 'expired' ones. Which approach enforces this in the database?
options: A CHECK constraint that counts the user's other active rows in a subquery
A foreign key from subscriptions.status to a statuses lookup table
A partial unique index on (user_id) with WHERE status = 'active'
questions.explanation: A partial unique index applies uniqueness only to the rows matching its WHERE clause. UNIQUE (user_id, status) would also limit each user to one cancelled row, CHECK constraints cannot contain subqueries, and a lookup foreign key only validates the status value.

questions.text: A CHECK constraint is added with NOT VALID to a table whose data already violates it. Which statement is the first to fail?
questions.explanation: NOT VALID adds the constraint without checking existing rows, so line 3 succeeds even though -1 violates it; the constraint is enforced for new rows, so line 4 fails. Without NOT VALID, line 3 would fail.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified on PG16.

questions.text: orders.customer_id references customers(id) with the default foreign key behaviour (no ON DELETE clause). What happens when you DELETE a customer who still has orders?
options: The DELETE fails with a foreign key violation
The DELETE succeeds and the orders keep the old customer_id
The DELETE succeeds and the orders are deleted too
The DELETE succeeds and customer_id becomes NULL on the orders
questions.explanation: The default action is NO ACTION: the delete is rejected (error 23503) so no orphaned orders can exist. Cascading, nulling or defaulting happens only when ON DELETE CASCADE, SET NULL or SET DEFAULT is declared.

questions.text: The query SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'ann@example.com' is slow on a table with ten million rows and no index on email. Which change is the most direct fix?
options: Run VACUUM FULL users before each query
Create a B-tree index on users (email)
questions.explanation: An equality lookup on an unindexed column forces a sequential scan; a B-tree index on that column lets PostgreSQL find the row directly. An index on another column, VACUUM FULL or a leading-wildcard LIKE does not help.

questions.text: On a large table EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan for the query on line 2, even though users_email_idx exists. Which change lets PostgreSQL use an index for this query?
questions.code_snippet:
1  CREATE INDEX users_email_idx ON users (email);
2  SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'ann@example.com';
questions.explanation: The index stores email, but the query filters on lower(email); a plain index cannot answer a condition on an expression. An expression index on lower(email) can. Sort direction, fresh statistics or the hash method on email do not change that.

questions.text: An orders table has 20 million rows; 99% have status 'shipped' and the app constantly reads the few rows with status 'pending'. Which index best serves WHERE status = 'pending' with the least storage and write overhead?
options: A full B-tree index on status
A partial index on status with WHERE status = 'pending'
A composite B-tree index on (status, created_at, total)
questions.explanation: A partial index contains only the rows matching its predicate, so it is tiny and is updated only when a pending row changes, yet it fully serves the pending lookups. The other indexes cover all 20 million rows.

questions.text: After ten more indexes were added to a busy events table, INSERT and UPDATE statements became slower while some SELECTs got faster. What is the most likely reason?
options: PostgreSQL re-sorts the whole table on every insert
Every write must also update each index on the table
Each index takes an exclusive table lock for the length of any query
PostgreSQL turns autovacuum off for tables with many indexes
questions.explanation: Indexes are extra structures that must be maintained on every INSERT, DELETE and non-HOT UPDATE, so each one adds write cost and storage. They do not re-sort the table, lock it for reads or disable autovacuum.

questions.text: A transfer runs UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1 and then UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2. Why should both statements run in one transaction?
options: So that either both changes are applied or neither is
So that the second statement runs faster
So that other sessions cannot read the accounts table meanwhile
Because a single statement cannot change more than one row
questions.explanation: A transaction makes the transfer atomic: if the second update fails, the first is rolled back instead of losing 100. Under MVCC readers are not blocked, and each statement is already atomic on its own.

questions.text: Starting balance is 100 and the default isolation level is overridden as shown. What happens at line 5?
options: It succeeds and sets the balance to 40
It succeeds and sets the balance to 90
It fails with a serialization failure (could not serialize access due to concurrent update)
It succeeds but changes nothing because A's snapshot is stale
questions.explanation: Under REPEATABLE READ, A works from the snapshot taken at its first query. Updating a row that another transaction changed and committed since then raises SQLSTATE 40001, and the application must retry. READ COMMITTED would instead re-read the row and give 40.

questions.text: Both sessions use the default isolation level and the balance starts at 100. B's UPDATE on line 5 has to wait. What is the balance after line 7?
questions.explanation: B blocks on A's row lock. When A commits, B re-evaluates its UPDATE on the newly committed row (100 - 30 = 70), so balance - 20 gives 50. Under READ COMMITTED no update is lost.

questions.text: Rows 1 and 2 exist. Each session already holds a row lock from its first UPDATE and now reaches line 4 and line 5. What does PostgreSQL do?
options: It detects the deadlock and aborts one transaction with an error
It aborts both transactions with an error
Both sessions wait forever until an administrator cancels one
Both updates succeed because each session sees its own row version
questions.explanation: Each session waits for a lock the other holds. PostgreSQL's deadlock detector notices the cycle (after deadlock_timeout, 1 s by default), aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40P01 and lets the other continue. The application should retry.

questions.text: A web API connects to PostgreSQL. To follow the principle of least privilege, which database role should it use?
options: The postgres superuser, so that migrations never fail
The owner of every table, so that any query can run
A dedicated role granted only the privileges it needs on the tables it uses
A role with CREATEROLE, so it can add users when needed
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits the damage of a bug or SQL injection. The application should use its own login role with only the needed grants, never a superuser, owner or role-creating account.

questions.text: Which statement takes the SELECT privilege on table orders away from role reporting?
options: DENY SELECT ON orders TO reporting
REVOKE SELECT ON orders FROM reporting
DROP SELECT ON orders FROM reporting
GRANT NO SELECT ON orders TO reporting
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL removes privileges with REVOKE. DENY is SQL Server syntax, and the other two are not valid PostgreSQL statements.

questions.text: Row-level security is enabled with an owner = current_user policy. Role alice is not the table owner. What does the SELECT on line 7 return for her?
questions.explanation: With RLS enabled, the policy filters the rows alice can see to those where owner = current_user: her two rows. Without the policy she would get the default deny (0 rows), and RLS applies to her because she is not the owner.

questions.text: Role bob created notes, so he owns it; he is not a superuser and has no BYPASSRLS. What does the SELECT on line 6 return when bob runs it?
questions.explanation: Table owners are exempt from row-level security unless the table is set to FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, so bob sees all 3 rows even though the policy would limit him to 1. Applications should connect as a non-owner role.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified on PG16: owner bypasses RLS without FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY.

questions.text: The policy has only a USING expression, and alice is not the owner. What happens when she runs the INSERT on line 6?
options: It fails: new row violates row-level security policy for table notes
It succeeds, but alice cannot see the new row afterwards
It succeeds and inserts 0 rows with no error
It fails with: permission denied for table notes
questions.explanation: A policy created without FOR defaults to ALL, and when WITH CHECK is omitted the USING expression is also applied to new rows. The row for 'bob' fails the check and the statement errors out. It is not a table privilege error because alice has INSERT.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified on PG16.

questions.text: A SaaS app keeps every customer's rows in shared tables with a tenant_id column. A bug could leave out the WHERE tenant_id = ... filter. Which feature makes the database itself enforce the tenant boundary?
options: A column-level GRANT on the tenant_id column
Row-level security policies that compare tenant_id with a per-session setting
questions.explanation: RLS policies filter every query on the table, whatever the application code does, and can read a session setting such as current_setting('app.tenant_id'). Grants, check constraints and unique indexes do not restrict which rows a role reads.
