questions.text: In React 18, what does automatic batching do?
options: Combines several state updates into one re-render, even inside timeouts and promises
questions.explanation: Since React 18, updates are batched everywhere, including inside timeouts, promises and native event handlers, so several setState calls in one tick cause a single re-render. Earlier versions batched only inside React event handlers.

questions.text: Why is mutating state directly (e.g. pushing into an array held in state) a problem?
options: React may not detect the change because the reference is the same
questions.explanation: React decides whether to re-render by comparing the new state with the old using Object.is. Pushing into the existing array keeps the same reference, so the change may not be detected. Create a new array (e.g. [...items, item]).

questions.text: What does React.lazy combined with Suspense provide?
options: Code-splitting: loading a component's code only when it is first rendered
questions.explanation: React.lazy loads a component through a dynamic import() the first time it renders, and Suspense shows a fallback while the chunk loads. This splits the bundle so users download less code up front. It is not SSR, state or memoisation.

questions.text: When does an effect with an empty dependency array (`useEffect(fn, [])`) run?
options: Only after the first render (and cleanup on unmount)
questions.explanation: With an empty dependency array the effect runs after the first render and its cleanup runs on unmount, since it has no values to react to. (In development StrictMode adds one extra mount/unmount cycle.)

verification.reviewer_note: Minor: in dev StrictMode the effect runs mount-cleanup-mount; the answer is still correct for normal semantics.

questions.text: What does calling a state setter from useState do?
options: Schedules a re-render with the new state
Resets every other piece of state
questions.explanation: A state setter queues an update and schedules a re-render with the new value. The variable in the current render keeps its old value, and other state is untouched.

questions.text: What is the purpose of React Context?
options: To pass values through the tree without passing props at every level
questions.explanation: Context lets a provider make a value available to any descendant through useContext, avoiding prop drilling through intermediate components. It is a delivery mechanism, not a replacement for state, a data-fetching tool or a speed-up.

questions.text: What does a component's return value of `null` mean?
questions.explanation: A component that returns null renders nothing in its place, which is the standard way to hide a component conditionally. It does not throw, unmount the parent or keep earlier output.

questions.text: Changing the `.current` value of a ref created with useRef will…
questions.explanation: A ref is a mutable box that persists across renders. Writing to ref.current does not notify React, so no re-render happens. Use state when the UI must update.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of useCallback?
options: To keep the same function identity between renders unless its dependencies change
questions.explanation: useCallback returns the same function instance between renders until its dependencies change. This matters for referential equality, e.g. when passing callbacks to React.memo children or listing them in effect dependencies.

questions.text: Why does React need a `key` prop on list items?
options: To identify items between renders so it can match and reorder them
questions.explanation: Keys give list items a stable identity so React can match items between renders, reorder DOM nodes and preserve each item's state. They are not passed as props and do not affect sorting, styling or focus.

questions.text: What is 'lifting state up'?
options: Moving state to the closest common parent of components that need it
questions.explanation: Lifting state up means moving shared state to the closest common ancestor and passing it down as props (with callbacks to change it), so sibling components stay in sync.

questions.text: Which hook memoizes a computed value between renders?
questions.explanation: useMemo caches the result of a computation between renders and recomputes it only when its dependencies change. useRef holds a mutable box, useId generates ids and useState holds state.

questions.text: What is a 'controlled' input in React?
options: An input inside a form tag
An input rendered by a server
An input whose value is driven by React state
questions.explanation: A controlled input gets its value from React state through the value prop and reports changes through onChange, so React is the single source of truth. An uncontrolled input keeps its value in the DOM.

questions.text: Which statement about the Rules of Hooks is correct?
options: Hooks can be called from class components
Hooks must be called inside conditions
Hooks must be called in the same order on every render, at the top level of components or custom hooks
Hooks may be called inside loops
questions.explanation: React identifies hooks by call order, so hooks must be called unconditionally at the top level of function components or custom hooks, in the same order every render. Not inside conditions, loops, nested functions or classes.

questions.text: Which is the safest way to render user-supplied text in React?
options: Rendering it as a child expression like {text}
questions.explanation: React escapes strings rendered as children ({text}), so user input is shown as text and cannot inject markup. dangerouslySetInnerHTML, HTML strings and eval can all execute attacker-controlled content.

questions.text: What should a useEffect cleanup function typically do?
options: Set state for the next render
Undo subscriptions, timers or listeners the effect created
questions.explanation: The cleanup function runs before the effect re-runs and when the component unmounts. It should release what the effect set up (subscriptions, timers, listeners, requests) to avoid leaks and stale callbacks.

questions.text: Which prop holds the elements written between a component's opening and closing tags, as in `<Card>...</Card>`?
questions.explanation: React passes whatever is nested between the tags as the special `children` prop. There is no built-in `content`, `slot` or `inner` prop; those names only work if the parent passes them explicitly.

questions.text: A child component must change a number that its parent owns and passes down as a prop. What is the idiomatic way?
options: The child assigns a new value to props.count, which makes React re-render the parent component
The parent also passes a callback prop; the child calls it and the parent updates its state
The child keeps the number in a module-level variable that the parent component reads on render
The child calls ReactDOM.render again with a different count prop for the same parent
questions.explanation: Props are read-only (frozen in development). Data flows down and changes flow up: the owner of the state exposes a setter or handler via props, the child calls it, and the owner re-renders with the new value.

questions.text: What HTML does `Inbox` produce when `messages` is an empty array?
questions.explanation: `messages.length && ...` evaluates to 0 when the array is empty, and React renders the number 0 as text (unlike false, null or undefined, which render nothing). Use `messages.length > 0 &&` or a ternary.

questions.text: What does `<Badge color={null} />` render?
questions.explanation: Destructuring defaults apply only when the value is undefined, not when it is null. With color={null} the default 'gray' is not used and string concatenation turns null into 'null'.

questions.text: After the button is clicked once, what text do the list items show, in order?
questions.explanation: With key={i} the rows are matched by position, not by item. After removing the first name, row 0 and row 1 keep their existing instances, whose `label` state was initialised once from the old props, so they still show A and B and the last row is unmounted. Use a stable id as the key.

questions.text: Typing in this input loses focus after every keystroke. What is the cause?
options: The onChange handler is an inline arrow function, which is recreated on every render and so resets the focus
The input is controlled, and React drops the focus from controlled inputs after each state update it applies
EmailField is declared inside SignupForm, so each render creates a new component type and remounts the input
useState is called before EmailField is defined, so the state update is lost and the input is re-created
questions.explanation: A component defined inside another component is a new function on every render, so React sees a different type, unmounts the old input and mounts a new one (losing focus). Declare EmailField outside SignupForm, or call it as a plain function. Inline handlers and controlled inputs do not cause this.

questions.text: The button is clicked twice while `first` is true, then `first` becomes false. What does the button show?
questions.explanation: Both branches render a Counter at the same position with the same type, so React keeps the existing instance and its state (n = 2) and only updates the label prop. Give the two a different key (or render them in different positions) to reset the state.

questions.text: `count` is 0. After one click on a button that runs `handleClick`, what is `count` on the next render?
questions.explanation: Both `setCount(count + 1)` calls use the same snapshot (count = 0), so each queues 'set to 1'. The updater `c => c + 1` then runs on the queued value 1 and gives 2. Use updater functions when the next state depends on the previous one.

questions.text: After clicking Add, the list on screen stays empty. Why?
options: The reducer returns the same state object it mutated, so React sees no change and skips the render
dispatch only schedules the update, so the list becomes visible after a second click on the button
useReducer cannot hold an array inside its state object, so the pushed item is silently discarded
The reducer must be wrapped in useCallback before dispatch will call it with the action object
questions.explanation: React compares the new state with the old using Object.is. A reducer that mutates `state` and returns it yields the same reference, so React bails out. Return a new object, e.g. { ...state, items: [...state.items, action.item] }.

questions.text: On the first click, which value does the timeout callback push onto `log`?
questions.explanation: Each render has its own snapshot of state. The handler created during the render where count is 0 closes over that 0, so the callback pushes 0 even though count becomes 5 on the next render.

questions.text: Two components each call the same custom hook `useCounter()`, which uses `useState` inside. How are their counters related?
options: They share one value, because the hook function is defined only once in the codebase
Each call gets its own independent state; the hook shares logic, not state
They share one value only if the two components are rendered as siblings in the tree
React throws an error when two different components call the same custom hook
questions.explanation: State created by useState inside a custom hook belongs to the component that calls it. Calling the hook twice gives two separate states. To share state, lift it up or put it in context.

questions.text: In a function component, where should a request that loads data when the component first appears normally be started?
options: Directly in the component body, before the return
Inside the JSX that the component returns
In the initial value, as useState(fetch(url))
questions.explanation: Rendering must be pure, so network requests belong in effects (or event handlers). Starting a request in the body would repeat it on every render, and useState(fetch(url)) would store a Promise.

questions.text: What does the dependency array in `useEffect(fn, [userId])` control?
options: The effect runs once for every item in the array, in the order that the items appear
userId is passed to fn as its first argument every time that the effect is run
React re-renders the component whenever userId changes, even when nothing else did
The effect runs again after a render only if userId changed since the previous render
questions.explanation: The array lists the reactive values the effect reads. After each render React compares them with the previous ones (Object.is) and re-runs the effect only if one differs. It does not pass arguments or trigger renders.

questions.text: The network tab shows this request being sent over and over. Which change stops the repeated requests while still loading the right user?
options: Pass [id] as the second argument to useEffect
Wrap the fetch call in a useCallback hook
Call setUser inside a setTimeout callback
Move the fetch call into the component body
questions.explanation: Without a dependency array the effect runs after every render; setUser with a new object triggers a render, which re-runs the effect, forever. [id] makes it run only when id changes. The other changes still fetch on every render.

questions.text: After the component has been on screen for about five seconds, what does it show?
questions.explanation: The effect runs once with an empty dependency array, so its callback closes over count = 0 forever. Every tick calls setCount(0 + 1), so the value becomes 1 and then stays 1. Use setCount(c => c + 1) or list count in the dependencies.

questions.text: A component mounts with id = 1 and is later re-rendered with id = 2 (no StrictMode). What does `log` contain afterwards?
questions.explanation: When the dependencies change, React first runs the cleanup of the previous effect (which closed over id 1), then runs the new effect with id 2. The cleanup therefore logs 'stop 1' before 'start 2'.

questions.text: `id` changes from 1 to 2 while the first request is pending, and the response for 1 arrives after the response for 2, so the screen shows user 1 under id 2. Which change fixes it?
options: Remove id from the dependency array so that only a single request is ever made
Wrap setUser in useCallback so that late responses are dropped before they apply
Set a local ignore flag in the effect's cleanup and skip setUser when it is set
Make the effect callback async and await the fetch call inside of that callback
questions.explanation: Responses can arrive out of order. A cleanup that sets `ignore = true` marks the earlier effect as stale, so its late response is discarded (AbortController works too). The other options either stop refetching, do nothing about ordering, or break the effect's return value.

questions.text: The component mounts (no StrictMode) and the button is then clicked twice. How many times is 'load' pushed onto `log`?
questions.explanation: `options` is a new object on every render, and dependencies are compared with Object.is, so the effect sees a changed dependency after each of the three renders (mount plus two clicks). Move the object outside the component or memoise it.

verification.reviewer_note: Assumes no StrictMode; in dev StrictMode the mount effect runs twice (log would get 4). Consider stating 'production build / no StrictMode' as effects-data-05 does.

questions.text: In development with StrictMode on, an effect that sends an analytics request on mount fires twice. What is the correct reading?
options: A mistake in the dependency array causes a second run of the effect in production builds too, not only in development
StrictMode doubles every state update, so production builds also render each component twice on mount
The browser fires the effect again whenever the tab regains focus after the user switches windows
React deliberately mounts, unmounts and remounts the component once in development to expose missing cleanup
questions.explanation: In React 18 development, StrictMode simulates unmount and remount once to check that effects are resilient (cleanup/idempotent). It does not happen in production builds. Fix by adding cleanup or making the effect safe to run twice, not by removing StrictMode.

questions.text: An input has `value={name}` but no `onChange` handler. What happens when the user types in it?
options: The text does not change, and React warns that the field is read-only
The text changes and name updates automatically as the user types in the field
The input is treated as uncontrolled and works normally without any warning
React throws an error and unmounts the whole form from the page
questions.explanation: Passing `value` makes the input controlled, so only state can change what it shows. Without onChange (or readOnly) the field is frozen and React logs a warning. Use defaultValue for an uncontrolled input.

questions.text: A `<form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>` handler does not call `event.preventDefault()`. What happens on submit?
options: React blocks the submit by itself and logs a warning to the console
The browser also submits the form normally, which reloads the page
Nothing extra happens, because React always cancels the default submission
The handler runs only after the browser has cleared the form fields
questions.explanation: React does not cancel the browser default for you. Unless the handler calls event.preventDefault(), the browser performs a normal form submission and reloads the page, losing client-side state.

questions.text: A sign-up form must show 'Email is invalid' only after the user has left the field, not while they are still typing. What is a good approach?
options: Disable the input until the user clicks Submit, then validate it and re-enable it for the next try
Store the error in a ref and read it during render so that the message appears a little later
Keep a touched flag per field, set it in onBlur, and show the error only if the field is touched and invalid
Throw an error from onChange and catch it in the parent component to display the message
questions.explanation: Validation logic can run on every change, but when to show the message is separate UI state. A per-field touched flag set on blur is the standard pattern. The other options block input, rely on refs that do not re-render, or misuse exceptions.

questions.text:
The user changes the field to 2. What does the `

` show?
questions.explanation: e.target.value is always a string, even for type="number". The state is the string '2', so qty + 1 concatenates to '21'. Convert with Number(e.target.value) before doing arithmetic.

questions.text: Users cannot type a space between their first and last name. What is the cause?
options: A controlled input with value={name} ignores whitespace characters that the user types into it
useState('') should start as null before the controlled input is able to accept spaces at all
onChange only fires on blur in React, so the typed space is dropped before the handler runs
trim() in onChange strips the space before it is stored, so the controlled value never contains it
questions.explanation: After typing 'John' and a space, the handler stores 'John ' trimmed to 'John', and React sets the input back to 'John', so the space disappears. Trim when submitting, not on each change.

questions.text: The form is submitted once with email 'bad'. What happens?
options: save('bad') is called, and the message 'Invalid email' appears
save is not called, and the message 'Invalid email' appears on the next render
save is not called, and no message appears because the update is still pending
save('bad') is called twice, and the message 'Invalid email' appears as well
questions.explanation: State updates are applied on the next render, so on line 7 `error` is still the empty string from this render's snapshot. `!error` is true, save runs with the bad email, and then the re-render shows the message. Validate into a local variable and branch on it.

questions.text: The console warns 'A component is changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled'. The input uses `value={user.name}`, which is undefined until the user loads. What is the best fix?
options: Add a defaultValue prop in addition to the value prop on the same input
Give the field a defined initial value, such as value={user.name ?? ''}
Remove the onChange handler so that the input is no longer controlled by state
Wrap the input component in React.memo so that its type can never switch
questions.explanation: An input whose value is undefined is uncontrolled; once the value becomes a string it switches to controlled, which React warns about. Always pass a string (an empty one while loading). Supplying both value and defaultValue also warns.

questions.text: Which tool shows how long each component takes to render and why it re-rendered?
options: The Elements panel in the browser's DevTools
questions.explanation: The React DevTools Profiler records commits, per-component render time and the reason for each render. The Elements panel shows DOM, StrictMode only adds development checks, and console.table prints data.

questions.text: ListView is wrapped in React.memo, yet it renders again on every keystroke. Why?
options: React.memo compares props only on the first mount and ignores them afterwards
React.memo does not work for components that render lists or other collections
A parent state update always forces every child to render, regardless of React.memo
The inline object literal is a new object on each render, so memo sees a changed prop
questions.explanation: React.memo skips rendering only if all props are Object.is-equal. `{ sort: 'asc' }` is a fresh object each render, so the comparison fails. Hoist it to a constant or memoise it with useMemo.

questions.text: Typing in a search box feels laggy because each keystroke re-renders a very large filtered list. Which React 18 feature keeps the input responsive by treating the list update as lower priority?
options: useDeferredValue (or startTransition) for the value that drives the list
flushSync around the state update that drives the list, so that it is applied right away
useLayoutEffect to filter the list before paint, so that the list is up to date at once
useId to give the list a stable identity, so that React can skip re-rendering its rows
questions.explanation: useDeferredValue and startTransition mark an update as non-urgent so React can interrupt it to handle urgent input first. flushSync does the opposite, useLayoutEffect blocks paint, and useId only generates ids.

questions.text: A table must show 20,000 rows and scrolling is slow. Which technique helps most?
options: Use each row's array index as its key, so that React can reuse the row elements
Windowing (virtualisation): render only the rows currently visible
Call forceUpdate on every row after it mounts, so the rows are painted quickly
Move the row data into Context so that each row updates on its own from the provider
questions.explanation: The cost is the number of DOM nodes and components. Windowing libraries mount only the visible slice plus a small buffer. Index keys, forced updates or context do not reduce the work, and some make it worse.

questions.text: A control saves a form and does not navigate anywhere. Which element should you use so that it works with the keyboard and screen readers by default?
questions.explanation: A native button is focusable, activates with Enter and Space, and is announced as a button. Links are for navigation, role="presentation" removes semantics, and tabIndex -1 removes the element from the tab order.

questions.text: In JSX, which attribute connects a `<label>` to the input whose id it names?
questions.explanation: `for` is a reserved word in JavaScript, so JSX uses htmlFor, which renders as the HTML `for` attribute. The label then names the input and clicking it focuses the input. The other names do not exist.

questions.text: Keyboard and screen-reader users cannot use this control. Which single change fixes both problems?
questions.code_snippet:
1
2 Save 3
options: Use <button type="button" onClick={handleSave}> instead of the div
Add an onKeyDown handler to the div that calls handleSave on Enter
questions.explanation: A native button is focusable, responds to Enter and Space, and exposes the button role. tabIndex alone makes it focusable but not operable or announced as a button; aria-label adds a name without role or keyboard support; onKeyDown adds one key but no role.

questions.text: After a failed submit, a React form renders an error message below the field. Screen-reader users hear nothing. Which change makes the message be announced?
options: Make the message red with a 4.5:1 contrast ratio
Render the message in an element with role="alert"
Set aria-hidden="true" on the message so it is not read twice
Give the message tabIndex={-1} and change nothing else
questions.explanation: Content inserted dynamically is not announced unless it is in a live region. role="alert" (or aria-live) makes assistive technology read it when it appears. Colour and contrast help sighted users, aria-hidden hides it, and tabIndex does not announce anything.

questions.text: A modal dialog opens when a button is clicked. Which behaviour gives keyboard users the correct experience?
options: Leave focus on the opening button and let Tab move through the page behind the dialog box
Move focus into the dialog and take every control out of the tab order so that Tab does nothing
Move focus into the dialog, trap Tab inside it, close on Escape, and restore focus to the trigger
Move focus to the first link of the page so that users can reach the site navigation from the dialog
questions.explanation: A modal must take focus, keep it inside while open, be dismissible with Escape and return focus to the control that opened it, otherwise keyboard users get lost behind the overlay. The other behaviours leave focus outside the dialog or make it unusable.

questions.text: Screen readers announce this input with no name. Which change gives it an accessible name?
questions.code_snippet:
1  <label>Email</label>
2  <input id="email" type="email" name="email" />
options: Change name="email" to name="Email" on the input
Add type="text" as well to the input element
Add role="label" as well to the label element
questions.explanation: A label only names an input when it is associated with it: htmlFor matching the input's id (or wrapping the input). The name attribute is for form data, type does not name anything, and there is no label role.

questions.text: In a single-page app, a route change swaps the content without a page load and screen-reader users get no cue. What is the recommended handling?
options: Move focus to the new page's main heading and update document.title
Call window.location.reload() on every route change to simulate a real page load
Put aria-live="assertive" on the app root so that all of its content is read out
Show a visual toast message for the change and leave the keyboard focus where it was
questions.explanation: A real navigation resets focus and announces the new title; a client-side route change does neither. Managing focus on the new heading and updating the title restores that. A root live region would read the whole page, and visual-only cues are invisible to screen readers.

questions.text: In React Testing Library, which query is generally preferred to find a button with the visible text 'Save'?
questions.explanation: Role queries find elements the way users and assistive technology do and also confirm the element is a real button. Class selectors and test ids are implementation details; `wrapper.find` belongs to Enzyme.

questions.text: What is the guiding principle of Testing Library?
options: Each component should be tested in isolation with all of its child components mocked out
Tests should assert the values of the internal state of every component that they render
Tests should resemble how users use the software, not test implementation details
Snapshots should replace explicit assertions so that tests never need to be updated by hand
questions.explanation: Testing Library encourages querying by role/label/text and asserting on what the user sees, so that refactors that keep behaviour do not break tests. Mocking all children, asserting state or relying on snapshots tie tests to implementation.

questions.text: After a click, a success message appears only once a mocked request resolves. Which query waits for the message to appear?
questions.explanation: findBy* queries return a promise that retries until the element appears or a timeout passes. getBy* and getAllBy* throw immediately if nothing matches; queryBy* returns null immediately.

questions.text: A component test passes locally but fails now and then in CI because it calls the real API. What is the best fix?
options: Mock the network layer (for example with MSW or a mocked fetch) so responses are fixed
Raise the timeout of every waitFor call in the test suite until the failures stop appearing
Retry the failed tests automatically in CI until one of the attempts finally passes
Run the affected test only on developer machines and skip it in the CI pipeline
questions.explanation: Tests that depend on a real network are non-deterministic. Mocking the network boundary gives fixed responses and still exercises the component. Longer timeouts and retries hide the flakiness instead of removing it.

questions.text: This test throws before reaching the assertion even though the banner is correctly hidden. What is the fix?
options: Use findByText on line 3, which waits for the banner to disappear from the document
Use queryByText on line 3, which returns null instead of throwing when nothing matches
Wrap line 2 in act, because render is asynchronous and the banner is hidden too late
Replace not.toBeInTheDocument with toBeFalsy and keep getByText as the query
questions.explanation: getByText throws if no element matches, so it cannot be used to assert absence. queryByText returns null, which not.toBeInTheDocument accepts. findByText also rejects when nothing appears, and wrapping render in act or changing the matcher does not stop getByText throwing.

questions.text: With user-event v14 this test fails with 'Unable to find an element with the text: Count: 1'. Which change fixes it?
options: Replace getByRole on line 3 with getByText, so that the button is found more reliably
Wrap the expectation on line 4 in act(() => { ... }), so that updates get flushed
Await the call on line 3, because user-event v14 methods return promises
Replace the matcher on line 4 with toBeTruthy, which is less strict about the element
questions.explanation: In v14 the user-event APIs are asynchronous, so the click has not been applied when line 4 runs. Awaiting it fixes the test. A different query, an act around the check, or a different matcher cannot make the click happen earlier.

questions.text: A test clicks `screen.getByTestId('submit')`. After a refactor the button became `<div data-testid="submit" onClick={...}>`; the test still passes but keyboard users can no longer submit. What does this show?
options: Tests should never click elements, and should call the component's handlers directly instead
The test needs a longer timeout so that the browser has time to focus the div element
data-testid attributes should be removed from the markup so that such tests fail sooner
Test-id queries can pass when the element is no longer accessible; role-based queries would catch it
questions.explanation: getByTestId finds the element regardless of its semantics, so it hides accessibility regressions. getByRole('button') would fail once the div lost its role. Calling handlers directly tests even less of what users do.

questions.text: A component debounces its search input by 300 ms. How can a unit test check the debounced call without really waiting 300 ms?
options: Use fake timers and advance them by 300 ms
Lower the delay to 0 in production code
Poll the assertion in a loop for ten seconds
questions.explanation: Fake timers (jest.useFakeTimers or vi.useFakeTimers) let the test control the clock and advance it instantly, so the test is fast and deterministic. Changing production delay, spamming the handler or long polling do not test the behaviour reliably.

competencies.name: Test design and boundaries
competencies.description: Choosing cases: equivalence classes, boundaries, negative and edge cases.

competencies.name: Unit testing
competencies.description: Isolated tests, fixtures, mocks and stubs, assertions and test doubles.

competencies.name: API and integration testing
competencies.description: Testing HTTP APIs and services together with a real database or stack.

competencies.name: End-to-end and UI testing
competencies.description: Browser tests, Playwright or Cypress, selectors and flaky tests.

competencies.name: Debugging and failure analysis
competencies.description: Reproducing bugs, reading failures, isolating causes and regressions.

competencies.name: Test automation and CI
competencies.description: Running tests in CI, pipelines, test data and keeping suites fast and reliable.

questions.text: In test-driven development (TDD), what comes first?
questions.explanation: Test-driven development follows red, green, refactor: write a failing test that states the wanted behaviour, make it pass with the simplest code, then clean up. Deployment, implementation-first and refactoring-first all break that order.

questions.text: Which statement about 100% code coverage is true?
options: It proves the code has no bugs
It shows every line ran, but not that behaviour is correct
questions.explanation: Coverage only records which lines or branches executed. A test with no meaningful assertion still raises coverage, so 100% neither proves the absence of bugs nor shows behaviour is correct. It is achievable, and it has no effect on test speed.

questions.text: What does code coverage measure?
options: How much code is executed by the tests
questions.explanation: Code coverage is the share of the code's lines, branches or functions that run while the tests execute. It does not count tests, bugs or speed.

questions.text: What is a test double such as a mock or stub used for?
options: Replacing a real dependency to isolate the code under test
questions.explanation: Mocks, stubs and fakes stand in for a real dependency such as a database, clock or network service, so the code under test runs in isolation, fast and deterministically.

questions.text: What is the testing pyramid's main idea?
options: Have many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and few end-to-end tests
questions.explanation: The testing pyramid advises many fast, cheap unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle and a small number of slow, brittle end-to-end tests at the top.

questions.text: What is an end-to-end (E2E) test?
options: A test that drives the full system the way a user would
questions.explanation: An end-to-end test exercises the whole running system through its real entry point, for example a browser clicking through a user flow, rather than a single function or layer.

questions.text: What should a good bug report include?
options: Steps to reproduce, expected result and actual result
questions.explanation: A useful bug report lets someone else reproduce and judge the problem: the steps to reproduce, what was expected and what actually happened. A fix or an opinion is not required.

questions.text: What is a flaky test?
options: A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without code changes
questions.explanation: A flaky test gives different results on the same code, usually from timing, shared state, ordering or external dependencies. Slow, skipped or assertion-free tests are different problems.

questions.text: What does a unit test check?
options: A small unit of code in isolation
The whole system end to end
questions.explanation: A unit test checks one small piece of code, such as a function or class, in isolation from the database, network and other components.

questions.text: What is a security test for IDOR checking?
options: That one user cannot access another user's resource by changing an id
questions.explanation: An IDOR (insecure direct object reference) test logs in as one user, requests another user's resource by changing an id in the URL or body, and expects a refusal such as 403 or 404.

verification.reviewer_note: Stem wording is awkward ('What is a security test for IDOR checking?'); answer is still unambiguous.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a test fixture?
options: Setting up a known state or data for tests
questions.explanation: A fixture builds the known starting state a test needs, such as sample data, a database row or a client, and usually tears it down afterwards, so tests are repeatable.

questions.text: What is fuzz testing?
options: Feeding unexpected or random inputs to find crashes and errors
questions.explanation: Fuzz testing feeds large amounts of malformed, unexpected or random input to a program to reveal crashes, hangs and unhandled errors.

questions.text: What does boundary value analysis focus on?
options: Values at and just around the edges of valid ranges
questions.explanation: Boundary value analysis picks test inputs exactly at, just below and just above the limits of valid ranges, because off-by-one mistakes cluster there.

questions.text: What is regression testing?
options: Re-running tests to make sure existing behaviour still works after changes
questions.explanation: Regression testing re-runs existing tests after a change to confirm that behaviour that used to work still works. It is the main job of an automated suite in CI.

questions.text: What is equivalence partitioning?
options: Splitting inputs into groups expected to behave the same and testing one from each
questions.explanation: Equivalence partitioning divides the input domain into classes expected to be handled the same way, then tests one representative per class instead of every value.

questions.text: What is property-based testing?
options: Generating many inputs to check that a stated property always holds
questions.explanation: Property-based testing, for example with Hypothesis or fast-check, states an invariant such as 'reversing a list twice returns the original' and checks it against many generated inputs, shrinking failures to a minimal case.

questions.text: A field accepts an age from 18 to 65 inclusive. Which set of inputs covers both sides of each boundary?
questions.explanation: Boundary value analysis tests just outside and exactly on each edge: 17 and 18 at the lower edge, 65 and 66 at the upper edge. The other sets miss at least one side of a boundary.

questions.text: Which of these is a negative test for a login form?
options: Sign in with valid credentials and check that the dashboard opens
Submit a wrong password and check that sign-in is refused
Check that the login page loads in under two seconds
Tick 'remember me' and check that the cookie lasts 30 days
questions.explanation: A negative test supplies invalid input or conditions and verifies the system refuses safely. The valid sign-in is a positive test, the load time a performance check and the cookie lifetime a positive feature test.

questions.text: A search page has three filters: category (4 options), stock status (2 options) and price band (3 options). What is the smallest number of tests that covers every pair of values taken from any two filters (pairwise coverage)?
questions.explanation: Category and price band alone have 4 x 3 = 12 distinct pairs, and one test covers only one such pair, so 12 is a lower bound. Assigning stock status alternately (for example (category + price) mod 2) covers its pairs too, so 12 suffices. 24 is all combinations, 4 only covers each value once.

verification.reviewer_note: Minimum is 4x3=12 (largest two factors), achievable since a 4x3 covering array with the binary factor exists.

questions.text: A mutation-testing tool changes `>=` to `>` in `if age >= 18`. The whole suite still passes, and the coverage report shows that line as executed. What does this most likely show?
options: The coverage report is wrong about that line
The code is correct, so no test needs to fail
Mutation testing cannot be applied to comparison operators
No test asserts the behaviour exactly at age 18
questions.explanation: The mutant changes behaviour only for age 18. A surviving mutant on an executed line means no test checks that exact value: the tests run the line but do not assert on the boundary. Mutation tools do handle relational operators, and passing here is a gap, not proof of correctness.

questions.text: The rule says shipping is free for orders of 50.00 or more. Which input exposes the defect in this function?
questions.explanation: The code uses `>` where the rule needs `>=`. Only an order of exactly 50.00 differs: the function charges 5 instead of 0. The other inputs give the right answer either way.

questions.text: Under the Gregorian rules, a year divisible by 400 is a leap year. These tests already pass: 2024 is leap, 2023 is not, 1900 is not. Which extra input is the only one of these that exposes the defect?
questions.code_snippet:
def is_leap(year):
    return year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0
questions.explanation: The function ignores the 'divisible by 400' exception, so it says 2000 is not a leap year. 2100 is correctly not leap, 2028 is leap by the plain rule and 1999 is not leap, so those give the right answer with the bug too.

questions.text: Which test fails when this file is run with pytest?
questions.explanation: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in binary floating point, so == 0.3 fails (pytest.approx is the fix). round(2.5) is 2 (round half to even), 7 // 2 is 3 and -7 // 2 is -4 (floor division), so those pass.

questions.text: What does pytest report for this test?
options: Passes: a ValueError is raised, and match ignores case by default
Passes: match is only checked when the exception type is wrong
Errors during collection: match needs a compiled regex pattern
Fails: the pattern does not match, as matching is case-sensitive
questions.explanation: pytest.raises(match=...) applies re.search to the exception text, which is case-sensitive. 'insufficient funds' does not contain 'Insufficient', so the test fails with 'Regex pattern did not match'. Using 'insufficient' or '(?i)Insufficient' would pass.

questions.text: A unit test patches every collaborator and asserts only that each mock was called, in a fixed order. After a refactor that keeps the behaviour identical, the test fails. What is the main weakness of this test?
options: It is tied to the code's internals, not to the behaviour it must provide
It uses too few mocks to isolate the unit from its collaborators
It should have been written as an end-to-end test instead
It lowers the code coverage figure that the pipeline reports
questions.explanation: Asserting on internal calls and their order couples the test to the implementation, so harmless refactors break it while real behaviour changes may slip through. Prefer asserting observable results or outputs; mock only the boundaries.

questions.text: pytest runs these two tests in file order. What is reported?
questions.explanation: A module-scoped fixture is created once and shared by every test in the module. test_add_one appends 1 and passes; test_add_two then sees a list that already holds 1, appends 2 and its length is 2, so the assertion fails. Function scope (the default) would isolate them.

questions.text: What happens when this test runs?
options: It passes: patch replaces fetch for every module that uses it
It fails with ModuleNotFoundError: util cannot be patched
It fails: service still calls the fetch it imported by name
It passes, but only when this test runs on its own, not in a suite
questions.explanation: `from util import fetch` binds the name fetch inside the service module. Patching util.fetch replaces the attribute on util only, so service.run() still calls the real function and returns 'real'. Patch where the name is looked up: patch('service.fetch').

questions.text: Which test fails under pytest?
questions.explanation: pytest.approx tolerance is relative to the expected value: 103 x 0.02 = 2.06, but the difference is 3, so test_rel_small fails. test_rel_big allows 10.01 (difference 1), test_float passes with the default 1e-6 relative tolerance and test_zero passes through the default 1e-12 absolute tolerance.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified: approx(103, rel=0.02) tolerance 2.06 < 3; approx(1e-13) passes via default abs=1e-12.

questions.text: What does this script print?
questions.explanation: With a list side_effect, each call returns the next item, but an exception instance in the list is raised instead of returned. The fourth call finds the list exhausted and raises StopIteration. The values are therefore 1, a caught ValueError, 3 and a caught StopIteration.

questions.text: A test requests GET /users/9999 and no such user exists. Which status should it expect?
questions.explanation: A well-formed request for a resource that does not exist is answered with 404. 401 means missing or invalid credentials, 500 is a server fault and 201 is for successful creation.

questions.text: What mainly separates an integration test of an API endpoint from a unit test of its handler function?
options: It must drive a real browser instead of calling the API directly
It measures only the response time of the endpoint under heavy load
It runs the endpoint with real parts such as the router and database
It checks the JSON shape of replies but never the stored data
questions.explanation: An integration test checks that components work together, for example request routing, validation and a real database, while a unit test isolates the function with doubles. Neither needs a browser, and integration tests commonly verify stored data too.

questions.text: Which API test best checks that a protected endpoint enforces authentication?
options: Call it with a valid token and expect 200
Call it with a valid token and check the response schema
Call it with an unsupported method and expect 405
Call it with no token and expect 401
questions.explanation: Enforcement is shown by a request that lacks valid credentials being rejected (401). The valid-token tests are happy paths and the 405 test checks method handling, not authentication.

questions.text: API integration tests share one database and pass alone but fail intermittently when run together, depending on order. What is the best fix?
options: Give each test its own data and clean up afterwards
Run the tests in the one fixed order that happens to pass
Add a short sleep before each request is sent
Reuse one shared user across all of the tests
questions.explanation: Order-dependent failures come from tests leaking state into each other. Isolating data per test, with a transaction rollback or cleanup, removes the cause. Fixing the order, sleeping or sharing more state only hides or worsens it.

questions.text: Which status code does this script print?
questions.code_snippet:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: int

@app.post("/items")
def create(item: Item):
    return item

client = TestClient(app)
response = client.post("/items", json={"name": "pen", "price": "abc"})
print(response.status_code)
questions.explanation: FastAPI validates the body against the Pydantic model before calling the handler. 'abc' cannot be parsed as an int, so it answers 422 Unprocessable Content with error details and the handler never runs.

questions.text: A frontend team and an API team want to catch a breaking change to a response shape before deploying, without a full shared environment. Which approach fits best?
options: Load tests that send thousands of requests at the API
Manual exploratory testing of the API after each release
Consumer-driven contract tests run against the API
Frontend unit tests that use hand-written mock data
questions.explanation: Contract tests record what a consumer relies on and check the provider against it in CI, so a breaking change fails before release. Frontend tests with hand-written mocks cannot notice when the real API changes.

questions.text: Integration tests run against in-memory SQLite, but production uses PostgreSQL. What is the main risk?
options: SQLite cannot hold a database in memory while a test is running
In-memory databases are always slower than a real database server
SQLite tests cannot use transactions or roll back between tests
Tests can pass where PostgreSQL would behave differently or fail
questions.explanation: A different engine differs in dialect, type strictness, constraint and locking behaviour, so a green run says little about production. Running the tests against the same engine, for example in a container, avoids this.

questions.text: The first test sets a dependency override and never removes it. Run in file order under pytest, what is reported?
questions.explanation: The first test sets app.dependency_overrides and never removes it. The override outlives the test, so in the second test current_user returns 'admin' and the endpoint answers 200, not 401. Clearing the overrides in a fixture teardown fixes it.

questions.text: An integration test sends 20 concurrent POST /orders requests for an item with stock 1 and expects exactly one 201. It sometimes sees two. Which defect does this point to?
options: Missing validation of the fields in the order request body
A race between reading the stock and updating it without locking
A wrong status code returned for out-of-stock orders
A missing database index on the orders table's key column
questions.explanation: Two requests read stock 1 before either writes, so both succeed: a check-then-act race. The cure is an atomic conditional update, a row lock or a constraint. Validation, status mapping or an index would not let two orders through.

questions.text: What happens when this script runs with TestClient at its default settings?
questions.code_snippet:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/boom")
def boom():
    raise RuntimeError("unexpected")

client = TestClient(app)
response = client.get("/boom")
print(response.status_code)
options: It prints 500 for the failed request
It prints 200 with an error body
It raises RuntimeError at the client.get call
questions.explanation: TestClient defaults to raise_server_exceptions=True, so an unhandled exception in the app is re-raised in the test instead of becoming a 500 response. To assert on the 500 itself, create TestClient(app, raise_server_exceptions=False).

verification.reviewer_note: Relies on TestClient raise_server_exceptions=True default (verified).

questions.text: In a Playwright test, which locator for a 'Submit' button is the most resilient to layout changes?
questions.explanation: Role and accessible-name locators follow what users and assistive technology see, so they survive DOM restructuring. Absolute XPath, positional CSS and screen coordinates break whenever the layout changes.

questions.text: Why is a fixed sleep, such as waiting 5 seconds, a poor way to wait in a UI test?
options: It wastes time and still fails on a slower page
It stops the page from loading its own resources
It lowers the coverage figures that the suite reports
Browsers block timers while a test is automating them
questions.explanation: A fixed delay is either too long, wasting time on every run, or too short on a slow machine, causing flaky failures. Waiting for a concrete condition, such as an element becoming visible, is both faster and more reliable.

questions.text: This Playwright test fails about one run in ten with an empty text. What is the best fix?
options: Catch the assertion error and ignore it
Configure the runner to retry the test five times
questions.explanation: textContent() reads the toast once, immediately after the click, before the app has rendered it. A web-first assertion such as expect(locator).toHaveText() polls until the condition holds or the timeout ends. A fixed delay stays flaky, and ignoring errors or retrying only hides it.

questions.text: Several Playwright tests sign in as the same shared user and edit its profile. They pass one at a time but fail when run in parallel. Which fix removes the cause?
options: Raise the action timeout to 60 seconds
Add a sleep so tests start a few seconds apart
Give each test or worker its own account
Make the tests share cookies between workers
questions.explanation: Parallel tests editing one account overwrite each other's state, so the failure is a data collision. Isolated accounts per test or worker remove the collision. Longer timeouts, staggered starts and shared cookies leave the shared state in place.

questions.text: On slow CI machines a Playwright click succeeds (the button was visible, enabled and stable) but nothing happens. The single-page app attaches its handlers only after its scripts finish loading. What is the most reliable fix?
options: Use `click({ force: true })` to skip the actionability checks
Raise the global test timeout to 10 minutes
Click the button twice in case the first is lost
Wait for a ready signal from the app, then click
questions.explanation: Actionability checks cover the DOM, not whether the app's JavaScript is attached. Waiting for an application-level readiness signal, such as a rendered element or flag set after hydration, makes the click safe. Forcing, longer timeouts and double clicks do not address it, and a second click may repeat the action.

questions.text: A visual-regression test compares screenshots. It passes on developers' laptops but fails in CI with tiny font and anti-aliasing differences. What is the best fix?
options: Create the baselines in the CI container and compare them there
Raise the allowed pixel difference until the failures stop
Skip the visual test whenever the pipeline runs it
Commit new baselines from each developer's own laptop each time
questions.explanation: Font rendering and anti-aliasing differ across operating systems and browser builds. Producing and comparing baselines in one pinned environment removes that noise without weakening the check. A 100% threshold disables it, skipping hides it and per-laptop baselines recreate the mismatch.

questions.text: Each test passes when run alone, but test_b fails when both run together. What is the cause?
options: pytest runs tests in random order by default
One default list is shared by all calls
pytest reuses the return value of the first test
Strings in assertions are compared by identity
questions.explanation: A mutable default argument is evaluated once at definition time, so tags keeps growing across calls: test_b sees ['x', 'y']. pytest runs tests in file order by default and does not reuse return values. The fix is tags=None and a new list inside the function.

questions.text: A bug appeared somewhere in the last 200 commits and a test reproduces it. What is the fastest way to find the commit that introduced it?
options: Read through the diff of every one of the commits
Revert the 200 commits, then re-apply them one at a time
Run git bisect, with the test as the good/bad check
Ask each author whether their commit caused it
questions.explanation: git bisect binary-searches the history, so about eight test runs find the culprit among 200 commits, and it can be automated with `git bisect run`. The other approaches take far longer or depend on guesses.

questions.text: A test passes on a developer's machine but fails in CI every time. What is the best first step?
options: Re-run the CI job several times until it finally passes
Mark the test as skipped while it runs in CI only, for now
Increase the number of automatic retries for that CI job
Compare the CI and local setups, then reproduce CI locally
questions.explanation: A consistent difference between environments has a cause that can be found: dependency versions, environment variables, time zone, locale, file paths or test data. Reproducing the CI setup, for example in the same container, reveals it. Re-running, skipping and retries hide the problem.

questions.text: This test passes on some runs and fails on others with no code change. Why?
options: Hash randomisation changes the set's iteration order per run
pytest shuffles the contents of sets before every test run
Two tests run in parallel and both change the same set
The assertion compares the two lists by identity, not by value
questions.explanation: Python randomises string hashes for each process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so a set of strings iterates in different orders between runs. The test depends on an unspecified order; compare sorted(colours) or use a list. pytest does not shuffle sets, nothing here runs in parallel and == compares values.

questions.text: A test fails about 1 time in 20. After a fix it passed once. How can you best judge whether the fix worked?
options: Accept the fix, since one passing run proves that it works
Run it hundreds of times and compare the failure rate
Run it three times and accept three green results as proof
Merge it and wait to see whether anyone complains about it
questions.explanation: With a 5% failure rate, a single run passes 95% of the time and three runs still pass about 86% of the time, so they prove little. Hundreds of runs under the same conditions give a measurable before and after comparison.

questions.text: A user reports that exports fail 'sometimes'. What is the most useful first step?
options: Rewrite the entire export module from scratch right away
Double every timeout that the export code uses
Find a failing case and shrink it to the smallest input
Close the report until someone can make it happen again
questions.explanation: A reliable reproduction, ideally the smallest input, turns a vague report into something testable and gives a failing test to guard the fix. Rewriting, timeouts and closing the report skip the diagnosis.

questions.text: Which order of pipeline stages gives developers the fastest useful feedback?
options: End-to-end tests first, then integration, then unit tests
Integration tests first, then lint, then unit tests
All tests in one slow stage, in random order
Lint and unit tests, then integration, then end-to-end
questions.explanation: Fail fast: cheap, quick checks run first so most mistakes are reported within a minute or two, and slower, broader suites run only for changes that passed them. Starting with the slowest tests delays the same feedback.

questions.text: A CI test run takes 40 minutes because 2,000 independent tests run one after another. Which change cuts the time without dropping coverage?
options: Run the tests on parallel workers
Delete the slowest tests from the suite
Run the full suite once a week instead of per commit
Disable the assertions in the slow tests
questions.explanation: Independent tests can run concurrently, so sharding them across workers or jobs shortens the wall-clock time while keeping every test. Deleting tests, running them rarely or removing assertions reduces what is verified.

questions.text: The deploy step runs even when tests fail. Which line is responsible?
questions.code_snippet:
1  jobs:
2    test:
3      runs-on: ubuntu-latest
4      steps:
5        - uses: actions/checkout@v4
6        - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
7        - run: pytest || true
8        - run: ./deploy.sh
questions.explanation: `pytest || true` makes the step exit 0 whatever pytest returns, so the job continues to deploy. Without `|| true`, a failing pytest step fails the job and later steps are skipped by default.

questions.text: A CI test calls a live payment sandbox, and builds fail whenever the vendor is down. What is the best change?
options: Retry the live call ten times before the build is marked as failed
Ignore every test failure that comes from that particular CI job
Stub the vendor and run a few live checks in a non-blocking job
Run the job only at times when the vendor is known to be running
questions.explanation: Blocking builds on a third party makes the suite unreliable. Fast stubs (kept honest with contract checks) give deterministic results, while a small separate live smoke job still detects vendor changes without blocking merges.

questions.text: A flaky test blocks merges several times a week. Which policy handles it best?
options: Automatically rerun every failing test in the suite five times
Delete the test permanently without writing a replacement
Turn off the required checks on the whole repository
Quarantine it, non-blocking, with an owner and a deadline
questions.explanation: Quarantine keeps the main signal trustworthy and unblocks the team, while ownership and a deadline make sure the root cause is fixed. Blanket reruns hide real failures, and deleting or disabling checks removes protection.

questions.text: Four CI jobs run integration tests in parallel against one shared database and fail at random. What is the most robust fix?
options: Give each job its own database or schema
Add random delays so the jobs rarely overlap
Retry the failing jobs until they pass
questions.explanation: Parallel jobs overwrite and delete each other's rows, so the failures are collisions on shared state. A separate database or schema per job, often a throwaway container, removes them. More connections, delays and retries leave the sharing in place.

questions.text: A CI step runs `pytest -m smoke`, but no test carries the smoke marker. With pytest at its default settings, what happens?
options: pytest finds nothing to run, exits with code 0 and the step passes
pytest deselects every test, exits with code 5 and the step fails
pytest exits with code 1, as if a test had failed
pytest exits with code 4 because the marker is unknown
questions.explanation: When no tests are collected or all are deselected, pytest exits with code 5 (no tests collected), which a CI step treats as a failure. Code 1 means test failures and code 4 a usage error; an unregistered marker used only in -m is not a usage error.

verification.reviewer_note: Verified: all tests deselected -> exit 5; -m does not check marker registration.

competencies.name: Usability principles
competencies.description: Heuristics, consistency, feedback, error prevention and user flows.

competencies.name: Layout and visual hierarchy
competencies.description: Grids, spacing, typography, hierarchy and responsive layouts.

competencies.name: Accessibility
competencies.description: Contrast, focus, labels, alt text and inclusive design (WCAG).

competencies.name: User research basics
competencies.description: Interviews, usability tests, personas and turning findings into decisions.

questions.text: What is information architecture?
options: How content is organised, labelled and navigated
questions.explanation: Information architecture is the structure, grouping and labelling of content so people can find things and understand where they are.

questions.text: Which is an example of Hick's law in practice?
options: Users read in an F pattern
More choices increase the time to decide
Bigger buttons are easier to hit
questions.explanation: Hick's law: decision time grows with the number and complexity of choices, so fewer, grouped options help users decide faster.

questions.text: What does progressive disclosure mean?
options: Showing advanced options only when they are needed
questions.explanation: Progressive disclosure keeps the interface simple by revealing advanced or rarely used options only when the user asks for them.

questions.text: What is the purpose of usability testing?
options: To watch real users attempt tasks and find problems in the design
questions.explanation: Usability testing observes representative users performing realistic tasks to find where the design confuses them.

questions.text: What is a primary benefit of a design system?
options: Consistent, reusable components and patterns across the product
questions.explanation: A design system provides shared components, patterns and guidelines, which keeps products consistent and speeds up design and development.

questions.text: What is the recommended minimum touch target size on mobile (WCAG and platform guidance)?
questions.explanation: Platform guidance recommends targets of about 44 px (Apple) or 48 dp (Material).

verification.reviewer_note: Ambiguous: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 (AA) sets the minimum at 24x24 CSS px; 44x44 is AAA (2.5.5) / Apple HIG (Material is 48dp). Since the stem says 'WCAG and platform guidance' and the topic is WCAG 2.2, A is defensible. Reword to 'recommended (AAA / platform) size' or drop 24 as a distractor.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a visible focus indicator?
options: Showing keyboard users where they are on the page
questions.explanation: A visible focus indicator shows keyboard and assistive-technology users which control is active; removing it breaks keyboard navigation (WCAG 2.4.7).

questions.text: What is a skeleton screen?
options: A placeholder layout shown while content loads
questions.explanation: A skeleton screen shows a placeholder of the layout while content loads, signalling progress and reducing perceived waiting time.

questions.text: Why respect the 'prefers-reduced-motion' setting?
options: Some users get dizzy or distracted by motion
questions.explanation: prefers-reduced-motion reflects a user's OS setting. Large animations can cause dizziness or nausea for people with vestibular disorders, so reduce or remove them.

questions.text: What is the main goal of a primary button style?
options: To show the single most important action on the screen
questions.explanation: The primary button marks the one main action, so the screen's hierarchy tells users what to do next. Secondary actions are styled with less emphasis.

questions.text: Why use sentence case and clear verbs on buttons (e.g. 'Save changes')?
options: They say exactly what will happen when pressed
questions.explanation: Clear verb labels like 'Save changes' tell users the outcome of pressing the button, unlike vague labels such as 'OK' or 'Submit'.

questions.text: Why should status never be shown by colour alone?
options: Colours are not allowed in forms
People with colour-vision deficiencies may not perceive it; add text or icons
questions.explanation: About 1 in 12 men has a colour-vision deficiency. Colour must be paired with text, icons or patterns (WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Colour).

questions.text: What minimum contrast ratio does WCAG 2.1 AA require for normal body text?
questions.explanation: WCAG 2.1 AA requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text.

verification.reviewer_note: Stem says WCAG 2.1; also unchanged in 2.2, fine.

questions.text: A good error message should…
options: Say what went wrong and how to fix it
questions.explanation: Good error messages are specific, polite and constructive: they explain what happened and what to do next.

questions.text: What should an empty state include?
options: A short explanation and the next action to take
questions.explanation: An empty state should explain what belongs there and give the next action, such as a button to create the first item.

questions.text: What does Fitts's law describe?
options: Time to reach a target depends on its distance and size
questions.explanation: Fitts's law: the time to reach a target grows with its distance and shrinks with its size, so important targets should be large and close.

questions.text: A project settings page has a 'Delete project' button right next to 'Edit'. Users sometimes delete projects by accident. Which change best follows usability principles?
options: Separate the button visually and offer undo or a confirmation that names the project
Make Delete the primary-coloured button so it is easier to find
Add a tooltip that explains what Delete does
Remove all confirmations so users can work faster
questions.explanation: Error prevention and error recovery are core usability heuristics. Putting a destructive action apart from safe ones and offering undo or a specific confirmation reduces slips. A prominent Delete button makes accidents more likely, and a tooltip is too easy to miss.

questions.text: Which technique most directly draws the eye to the most important element on a screen?
options: Giving every element the same size and weight
Making it noticeably larger or higher in contrast than its surroundings
Surrounding it with several decorative borders
Setting it in a smaller font than the rest
questions.explanation: Visual hierarchy comes from differences in size, weight, colour and contrast. When everything looks the same nothing stands out, and decoration or smaller type does not lead the eye.

questions.text: In a form, labels sit midway between two fields, so it is hard to tell which field each label belongs to. Which fix applies the principle of proximity?
options: Put every label and field inside a border
Place each label closer to its own field than to the neighbouring field
Use a different colour for each label
questions.explanation: The Gestalt principle of proximity says elements that sit close together are perceived as a group. Moving each label nearer to its field than to the next one removes the ambiguity. Bold, borders and colour do not fix the spacing.

questions.text: Why do design teams define a spacing scale (for example 4, 8, 16, 24 and 32 px) instead of choosing margins freely?
options: Browsers only render spacing values that are multiples of 4
It removes the need for responsive layouts
It gives the layout a consistent rhythm and makes screens predictable
questions.explanation: A limited, consistent scale of spacing values makes related elements align, creates a visible rhythm and speeds up design decisions. It has no effect on rendering limits, speed or responsiveness.

questions.text: A card shows a title, three lines of metadata and two buttons, all in the same size, weight and colour. Users cannot tell what matters. Which redesign is best?
options: Use two or three distinct levels of size, weight and colour, with one clearly primary action
Make every piece of text bold so that nothing is missed
Add more content to the card to explain the hierarchy
Give both buttons the same bright colour so both stand out
questions.explanation: A clear hierarchy ranks content: a prominent title, de-emphasised metadata and a single visually dominant primary action. Emphasising everything or competing buttons removes contrast and recreates the problem.

questions.text: An app uses the same red for its main 'Pay now' button, for error messages and for the 'Delete' action. What is the design problem?
options: Red buttons are never allowed to be primary
Red is overloaded: it signals danger and errors, so it blurs the meaning of the primary action
Users cannot see red text on white backgrounds
A page may use only one button colour
questions.explanation: Colour carries meaning. Red is widely read as error or destructive, so using it for the main positive action, and also for deletion, makes users hesitate and weakens the hierarchy. Use distinct semantic colours for primary actions and danger.

questions.text: A screen reader announces only 'button' for this control. What is the right fix?
questions.code_snippet:
<button class="icon-btn">
  <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true">...</svg>
</button>
options: Add a title attribute to the svg element
Increase the size of the icon
Give the button an accessible name, such as aria-label="Delete message"
Remove the button and use a div with an onclick handler
questions.explanation: A button with only an icon has no text for assistive technology. An accessible name from visible or visually hidden text, or an aria-label, tells users what it does. A div without role and keyboard support would be worse, and size does not help.

questions.text: A modal dialog opens, but keyboard focus stays on the page behind it, and Tab moves through hidden page controls. What is the correct behaviour?
options: Leave focus where it is so users keep their place
Move focus to the browser address bar
Disable the Tab key on the whole page
Move focus into the dialog, keep Tab inside it while open, and return focus to the trigger on close
questions.explanation: Keyboard and screen-reader users must be taken into a modal, kept inside it (focus trap) and returned to the triggering element afterwards. Leaving focus behind makes the dialog unreachable and exposes content that is visually covered.

questions.text: A form fails validation. Which approach makes the errors accessible to screen-reader users?
options: Describe each error in text next to its field, link it with aria-describedby and move focus to the first error
Turn the invalid fields' borders red and shake them
Show a toast that disappears after three seconds
Show one 'Form invalid' alert at the top that does not name the fields
questions.explanation: Errors must be perceivable without colour or timing and tied to the field they concern. Text next to the field, programmatically associated with it, plus moving focus or announcing the error, lets assistive technology users find and fix each problem.

questions.text: What is a user persona?
options: A real customer who is legally bound to the product
A fictional but research-based profile that represents a group of users
A test script for usability sessions
A marketing slogan for a target audience
questions.explanation: Personas summarise goals, needs and behaviours of a user segment, based on research data, so teams can design for real people instead of themselves. They are not real individuals, scripts or slogans.

questions.text: Analytics show that many users abandon checkout at the payment step. Which method best reveals why?
options: Count page views of the payment page for another month
Run an A/B test of the button colour
Observe users attempting checkout in usability tests and interview them
Send a satisfaction survey with a 1 to 5 rating
questions.explanation: Analytics tell you where users drop off but not why. Watching people attempt the task and asking them about it exposes confusion, missing options or trust problems. Page counts, colour tests and generic ratings do not explain the cause.

questions.text: Which question is best for an interview that aims to understand how freelancers currently find work?
options: Would you use a feature that finds clients for you?
Don't you think finding clients is too difficult?
Do you find clients online, yes or no?
Tell me about the last time you looked for a new client.
questions.explanation: Open questions about specific past behaviour give reliable, detailed answers. Hypothetical questions are unreliable, leading questions bias the answer, and closed yes/no questions give little insight.

questions.text: A team wants to learn how users naturally group the sections of a new help centre. Which method fits?
questions.explanation: In card sorting, participants group labelled cards into categories they find logical, which informs the information architecture and navigation labels. A/B tests compare variants, heatmaps show interaction on a finished page, and audits check compliance.

questions.text: After one day an A/B test with 40 visitors shows variant B with a 12% higher sign-up rate, and a stakeholder wants to ship B immediately. What is the main problem?
options: A/B tests must always run for exactly one year
The sample is too small to tell a real difference from random variation
Variant B cannot win if it was shown second
Sign-up rate is never a valid metric
questions.explanation: With so few visitors the difference is well within chance. Decide the sample size or duration beforehand and test for statistical significance before concluding. Stopping early on a lucky streak is a classic mistake.

questions.text: In a survey, 80% of users say they would use a new 'export to PDF' feature, but analytics show almost nobody uses the existing 'export to CSV' button. What is the best next step?
options: Build the feature immediately, because the survey is definitive
Discard the survey results and rely only on analytics
Observe real behaviour with interviews or tests before building, since stated wishes often differ from actual use
Run the survey again with more questions
questions.explanation: People often report preferences that do not match their behaviour. Combining what users say with what they do, and investigating the gap with observation or interviews, gives a more reliable basis than either source alone.
